The report gives cost and performance results for pulverized coal (PC) and natural gas combined cycle (NGCC) power plants, all assessed on one consistent technical and economic basis intended to reflect current market conditions. Its main value is not the absolute accuracy of each capital cost estimate (judged to be -15%/+30%) but the uniform method, which makes the relative costs of the cases comparable. It belongs to an update of Volume 1 of a four-volume set: Volume 1 (Bituminous Coal and Natural Gas to Electricity); Volume 2 (Coal to Synthetic Natural Gas and Ammonia, various coal ranks), Volume 3 (Low Rank Coal and Natural Gas to Electricity) and Volume 4 (Bituminous Coal to Liquid Fuels). All PC and NGCC cases were updated and together form Volume 1a; the IGCC cases, which were combined with PC and NGCC in Revision 2a, are to be issued separately as Volume 1b. A revision control table in Section 6 lists the changes.

Six plant configurations are studied: four PC cases (two subcritical and two supercritical (SC), each with and without CO2 capture) and two NGCC plants built around state-of-the-art 2013 F-Class combustion turbines (with and without CO2 capture). Although called SC, the SC steam conditions used here, especially the 1100°F temperature, are broadly typical of commercial ultra-supercritical (USC) units; since efficiency depends more on steam temperature than on pressure, the resulting performance matches or nearly matches the best commercially offered USC PC plants. CO2 capture uses the Shell Cansolv system, which is based on an amine solvent. Exhibit ES-1 summarizes the case configurations.

Exhibit ES-1 Case configuration summary (columns: unit cycle; steam cycle psig/°F/°F; combustion turbine; boiler technology; CO2 separation). B11A: unit cycle=PC; steam cycle=2400/1050/1050; combustion turbine=N/A; boiler technology=Subcritical PC; CO2 separation=N/A. B11B: unit cycle=PC; steam cycle=2400/1050/1050; combustion turbine=N/A; boiler technology=Subcritical PC; CO2 separation=Cansolv. B12A: unit cycle=PC; steam cycle=3500/1100/1100; combustion turbine=N/A; boiler technology=SC PC; CO2 separation=N/A. B12B: unit cycle=PC; steam cycle=3500/1100/1100; combustion turbine=N/A; boiler technology=SC PC; CO2 separation=Cansolv. B31A: unit cycle=NGCC; steam cycle=2400/1050/1050; combustion turbine=2 x State-of-the-art 2013 F-Class; boiler technology=HRSG; CO2 separation=N/A. B31B: unit cycle=NGCC; steam cycle=2400/1050/1050; combustion turbine=2 x State-of-the-art 2013 F-Class; boiler technology=HRSG; CO2 separation=Cansolv.

Every configuration is assumed to be built on a greenfield site, with capacity factors (CF) set at 85%, taken as roughly equal to availability; reaching such CFs implies the plants sit near the top of the dispatch order. The target nominal net output is 550 MW. Because NGCC combustion turbines (CT) come only in discrete sizes while PC boilers and steam turbines can be had in almost any capacity, all PC cases deliver 550 MW net, whereas the NGCC cases deliver 559 MW (with capture) and 630 MW (without capture).

Emission requirements take the Hg and HCl limits from the Utility Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) as revised in March 2013 and the PM, SO2 and NOx limits from the New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) as revised in February 2013. In every PC case PM is caught in a baghouse, SO2 in wet flue gas desulfurization (FGD), mercury by dry sorbent injection (DSI) combined with activated carbon injection (ACI), and NOx by selective catalytic reduction (SCR) downstream of low NOx burners (LNB) fitted with overfire air (OFA). Both NGCC cases control NOx with LNBs and an SCR. All capture configurations are designed for 90 percent CO2 capture, leaving atmospheric CO2 emissions well below the proposed EPA rule; a footnote explains that EPA proposed a CO2 new source performance standard for new fossil-fired electric generating units on April 13, 2012, published in the Federal Register, with a limit of 1,100 lb-CO2/MWh-gross.

Steady-state models of all six plants were built in Aspen Plus® (Aspen). Equipment performance and process limits came from published reports, vendor and user information, data from design/build utility projects and/or engineering judgment. Vendors contributed to different extents to the updates to PC emission control equipment and, for both PC and NGCC plants, to CO2 capture, CO2 compression and steam turbine technology, but the final cost and performance assessment was made independently and carries no vendor endorsement. Aspen mass and energy balances were used to size the main equipment, and those sizes were the basis for costing; WorleyParsons estimated capital and operating costs for major equipment and subsystems from the simulation results and by scaling from earlier design/build projects.

Fuel prices (stated in 2011 U.S. dollars, as delivered to the Midwest and on a higher heating value (HHV) basis) are $2.78/GJ ($2.94/MMBtu) in the case of Illinois No. 6 coal and $5.81/GJ ($6.13/MMBtu) in the case of natural gas, as set in the QGESS document on fuel prices for NETL studies. The cost metric is the cost of electricity (COE): the revenue per net megawatt-hour the generator must earn to achieve the target internal rate of return on equity. COE is taken to rise each year at the general inflation rate, so it is constant (levelized) in real terms over the plant life. A CO2 transport and storage (T&S) cost of $11 per tonne of CO2 is added to the COE, representing a 62 km (100 mile) pipeline and storage in a Midwest deep saline formation, estimated with the FE/NETL CO2 Transport Cost Model and the FE/NETL CO2 Saline Storage Cost Model (see the May 2014 QGESS on CO2 transport and storage costs).

How the various fossil technologies compare on cost and performance will shape which mix is used to serve future power demand. Choice of new generating technology will hinge on factors such as capital and operating costs, fuel prices, overall energy efficiency, COE, availability, reliability and environmental performance, present and future rules on air, water and solid waste discharges from fossil plants, and the market uptake of clean coal technologies matured through recent commercial-scale demonstrations under DOE's Clean Coal and Carbon Management Program.

Key performance findings: the NGCC cases are the most efficient of all, at 51.5 percent without capture and 45.7 percent with capture, followed by the non-capture SC PC case at 40.7 percent. Adding CO2 capture lowers PC efficiency by 20 percent in relative terms (8 percentage points) and the NGCC case 11 percent (6 percentage points). The NGCC penalty is smaller because natural gas carries less carbon than coal (32 lb carbon/MMBtu of heat input versus 56 lb/MMBtu for the study fuels) and because the more efficient non-capture NGCC emits less CO2 for the same net output (about 54-56 percent less than the PC cases), leaving less CO2 to capture and compress. These advantages are partly cancelled by the leaner CO2 in NGCC flue gas (4% versus 13% for PC); per lb of CO2 captured, the energy penalty is 0.16 kWh for NGCC and 0.13 kWh for PC. Estimated Hg, PM, NOx and SO2 emissions all meet or fall below the regulatory limits now in force. Exhibit ES-3 is a graph of net plant efficiency (HHV basis) (Source: NETL).

Key cost findings: on a total overnight cost (TOC) $/kW basis, NGCC capital cost is about 34% (non-capture) and 42% (capture) of PC capital cost. Subcritical and SC PC capital costs are effectively the same within the study accuracy at fixed output. Normalized to equal net output, CO2 capture raises capital cost by 74% for PC and 115% for NGCC. NGCC COE is 70% (non-capture) and 61% (capture) of PC COE, and the SC versus subcritical PC COE difference is minor relative to the estimate accuracy. Capital is the largest COE component for PC (46-51 percent of COE; 21-31 percent for NGCC), while fuel dominates NGCC COE (53-71 percent; 22-31 percent for PC). CO2 T&S adds $4/MWh (NGCC) to $10/MWh (PC), under 7 percent of total COE in every capture case. Capture raises NGCC COE by 52 percent versus about 75 percent for PC.

Even with higher efficiency and a smaller COE increase, NGCC has higher costs of CO2 captured and avoided than PC, because less CO2 is available and at lower concentration; the avoided costs are effectively equal within report accuracy, with NGCC 3-5 percent above PC. If future legislation puts a price on carbon emissions, every technology studied becomes more costly, with non-capture plants hit harder than capture plants and coal plants hit harder than gas plants. Exhibit ES-5 shows COE broken down by cost component (Source: NETL; non-capture cases use conventional financing and the others high-risk financial assumptions per the QGESS cost estimation methodology).

Exhibit ES-6 plots COE (including CO2 T&S, $/MWh, 2011$) for the SC PC and NGCC cases against delivered natural gas price ($3 to $20/MMBtu). Bands for the SC PC cases (SCPC w/ CCS and SCPC w/o CCS at $2.94/MMBtu coal) span coal prices of $2.21 - $3.69/MMBtu, i.e. ±25% of the study value, revealing where NGCC competes with SCPC with and without CCS as gas price changes. For instance, with coal at $3/MMBtu, non-capture SC PC and non-capture NGCC reach equal COE at about $10.0/MMBtu gas, and the capture versions reach equal COE at $3.0/MMBtu coal and about $13.5/MMBtu gas (Source: NETL).

Selling the captured CO2 for use and storage in CO2 enhanced oil recovery (EOR) could create revenue for both the SC PC and NGCC capture plants, with the plant-gate price set by factors such as location and crude oil price. Exhibit ES-7 (lowest cost technology options at various natural gas and CO2 sales prices; Source: NETL) presents this as a 'phase diagram' whose lines mark COE parity between pairs of technologies. It shows that non-capture plants are cheapest below a first-year CO2 price of $56/tonne ($51/ton), and that NGCC wins when gas is under $10/MMBtu and CO2 revenue under $56/tonne (at 85 percent capacity factor). The gas price for parity among the NGCC and PC cases falls as CO2 revenue rises, reaching $6/MMBtu at roughly $100/tonne ($91/ton).

paragraphs.section: Executive Summary: Special Considerations on Reported Costs
paragraphs.text: Capital cost estimates carry an uncertainty of -15%/+30%, matching AACE Class 4 (feasibility study) estimates for the depth of design done. Each case aims to represent the next commercial offering, relies on vendor cost estimates for component technologies, and adds process contingencies at subsystem level to cover expected but undefined costs, which is harder for emerging technologies. Designs built only from fully mature, widely deployed technologies (e.g., PC and NGCC without CO2 capture) are costed as nth-of-a-kind (NOAK); such plants have become cheaper through learning by doing, serial-deployment risk reduction and ongoing R&D. Designs with not-yet-mature technology (any CO2 capture plant) are costed the same way, which does not fully capture the premiums of first complex commercial integrations, so early capture plants may cost more than reported. Real projects will also differ because of project- and site-specific factors (contracting strategy, local labor, seismic conditions, water quality, financing, local environmental issues, weather delays, etc.) not covered by the stated uncertainty. Further RD&D is expected to yield more advanced designs with lower costs than estimated here.

Chapter 1 states the aim of the report: to judge independently and accurately how much plants burning pulverized coal (PC) and natural gas combined cycle (NGCC) units cost and how they perform, done with one consistent technical and economic method that reflects present market conditions. The document updates Volume 1 of the four-volume series (Volume 1: Bituminous Coal and Natural Gas to Electricity; Volume 2: Coal to Synthetic Natural Gas and Ammonia (Various Coal Ranks); Volume 3: Low Rank Coal and Natural Gas to Electricity; Volume 4: Bituminous Coal to Liquid Fuels). Updated PC and NGCC results make up Volume 1a, while the IGCC cases that Revision 2a had grouped with PC and NGCC are moved into a separate Volume 1b; Section 6 holds the revision control table. The factors listed as governing the choice of new generating technology are capital and operating costs, overall energy efficiency, fuel prices, Cost of Electricity (COE), availability, reliability and environmental performance, current and future rules on air, water and solid waste discharges, and the market penetration of clean coal technologies matured through commercial-scale demonstrations in DOE's Clean Coal and Carbon Management Program.
terms: Clean Coal and Carbon Management Program

paragraphs.text: The study covers six plant configurations: four PC cases (two subcritical, two supercritical (SC), each with and without CO2 capture) and two NGCC plants based on state-of-the-art 2013 F-Class combustion turbines, with and without CO2 capture. The steam conditions labelled SC are in practice close to those of commercial ultra-supercritical (USC) plants, particularly the 1,100°F temperature, and because steam temperature affects efficiency more than steam pressure does, the SC results sit at or close to the best commercially available USC PC units. The Shell Cansolv CO2 capture process used throughout is an amine-based solvent system, and Exhibit 1-1 summarizes the cases. Vendors provided input to differing degrees for the updated PC pollution control equipment and for CO2 capture, CO2 compression and steam turbine technology in both PC and NGCC plants, yet the final cost and performance results were set independently and are not vendor-endorsed.

Exhibit 1-1 lists the plant configurations, and each case chapter describes its components in more detail. Gross and net output differ between the two NGCC cases because combustion turbine (CT) size is fixed: the state-of-the-art 2013 F-class CT modeled has a standard rating of 211 MW at International Standards Organization (ISO) conditions, and two CTs per case give 422 MW gross. A heat recovery steam generator (HRSG) recovers heat from the CT exhaust to drive a steam turbine. With capture, net output falls substantially because the CO2 capture system draws a large auxiliary power load and a large amount of extraction steam. Although the CTs supply 422 MW gross in both NGCC cases, total combined cycle gross output is 601 to 641 MW and net output 559 MW (Case B31B) to 630 MW (Case B31A), with the natural gas feed fixed at 84,134 kg/hr (185,484 kb/hr) in both.

Every PC case delivers 550 MW net, achieved by raising the coal feed rate in the capture cases. Boiler and steam turbine makers have shown commercially that they can size units to a custom specification, which allows the PC cases to be compared at a common net output; in the capture cases more coal is fired so the steam turbine produces more gross power and offsets the higher auxiliary load, keeping net output constant. The rest of the report is arranged as follows: Chapter 2 sets out the technical, environmental and cost evaluation basis; Chapter 3 describes the PC technologies and results for the four PC cases; Chapter 4 does the same for the two NGCC cases; Chapter 5 compares NGCC and PC cases; and Chapter 6 records report revisions.

Exhibit 1-1 Case descriptions (columns: unit cycle; steam cycle psig/°F/°F; combustion turbine; boiler technology; oxidant; sulfur removal/recovery; PM control; NOx control; CO2 separation; old case name in parentheses). B11A (9): unit cycle=PC; steam cycle=2400/1050/1050; combustion turbine=N/A; boiler=Subcritical PC; oxidant=Air; sulfur removal=Wet FGD/Gypsum; PM control=Baghouse; NOx control=LNB w/OFA and SCR; CO2 separation=N/A. B11B (10): same as B11A except CO2 separation=Cansolv. B12A (11): unit cycle=PC; steam cycle=3500/1100/1100; combustion turbine=N/A; boiler=SC PC; oxidant=Air; sulfur removal=Wet FGD/Gypsum; PM control=Baghouse; NOx control=LNB w/OFA and SCR; CO2 separation=N/A. B12B (12): same as B12A except CO2 separation=Cansolv. B31B (14): same as B31A except CO2 separation=Cansolv. Note A: the old case numbers from earlier editions are shown next to the new ones. Note B: all cases have a nominal 90 percent removal rate based on total feedstock carbon less unburned carbon in ash (PC cases); the capture rate from the flue gas in the Cansolv systems varies (explained in Section 2.4.3); all cases sequester CO2 offsite.

For every configuration an Aspen Plus® (Aspen) model was built to produce material and energy balances, which provided the design basis for the major equipment list; that list and the material balances in turn underpin the cost estimates for capital and operation. Limits on performance and process were drawn from published reports, vendor and user information, design/build utility project data, and/or engineering judgment, and WorleyParsons estimated capital and operating costs from the simulation results and by scaling earlier design/build projects. The figure-of-merit reported for revenue requirement is a COE computed for each case. The remainder of Chapter 2 covers the design basis shared by all technologies plus the environmental targets and cost assumptions; technology-specific criteria appear in later chapters.

All plants are placed at a generic Midwestern U.S. site whose characteristics and ambient conditions are given in Exhibit 2-1 and Exhibit 2-2; the ambient conditions equal ISO conditions. Exhibit 2-1 Site characteristics (Parameter: Value). Note A: the cooling water temperature is the exit temperature of cooling water from the cooling tower, set 8.5°F above the ambient wet bulb in ISO cases.

For PC cases the plant itself is taken to need 30 acres, with the remaining land forming a buffer of about 0.25 mi to the fence line that could also hold a rail loop if needed (no rail loop is included). For NGCC cases the plant proper is about 10 acres with a 0.15 mi buffer to the fence. The steam turbine is housed in a turbine building in all cases and the boiler is also enclosed in the PC cases, while the NGCC CTs are left unenclosed. Several design parameters are treated as site-specific and are not quantified, with allowances for normal conditions and construction carried in the cost estimates: seismic design, flood plain issues, reuse and discharge of water, the soil and site conditions already present, criteria for rain and snow, buildings/enclosures, local height codes, noise regulations affecting the site and surroundings, other local environmental concerns, and weather delays.

Illinois No. 6 is the design coal (Exhibit 2-3), with properties taken from the January 2012 revision of the Quality Guidelines for Energy System Studies (QGESS) document "Detailed Coal Specifications." Capital charge factors (CCF) were obtained with the Power Systems Financial Model (PSFM), which needs every cost input on the same cost-year basis; since capital and operating costs are in June 2011 dollars, fuel costs are also expressed in June 2011 dollars. The coal price assumed is $2.78/GJ ($2.94/MMBtu), HHV basis, delivered to the Midwest, in 2011 U.S. dollars (per the November 2012 QGESS on fuel prices for NETL studies).
terms: Quality Guidelines for Energy System Studies (QGESS)

paragraphs.text: Exhibit 2-3 Design coal. Rank=Bituminous; Seam=Illinois No. 6 (Herrin); Source=Old Ben Mine. Proximate analysis (weight %; as received / dry): Moisture=11.12 / 0.00; Ash=9.70 / 10.91; Volatile Matter=34.99 / 39.37; Fixed Carbon=44.19 / 49.72; Total=100.00 / 100.00; Sulfur=2.51 / 2.82; HHV, kJ/kg (Btu/lb)=27,113 (11,666) / 30,506 (13,126); LHV, kJ/kg (Btu/lb)=26,151 (11,252) / 29,544 (12,712).
