Across 34 samples of Illinois No. 6 coal shipped by Illinois mines, mercury averaged 0.09 ppmwd (arithmetic mean) with a standard deviation of 0.06, so as Exhibit 2-4 shows there is a 50 percent chance the coal's mercury does not exceed 0.09 ppmwd. The report uses 0.15 ppmwd for all PC cases, i.e. mean plus one standard deviation, covering about 84 percent of samples, and assumes all coal Hg goes to the gas phase with none leaving in the bottom ash. Exhibit 2-4 Probability distribution of mercury concentration in the Illinois No. 6 coal (cumulative probability that a sample is at or below a given mercury concentration in coal, ppm db; arithmetic mean = 0.09 ppm db, standard deviation = 0.06 ppm db; Source: NETL).

Cases B31A and B31B (NGCC with and without CO2 capture) burn natural gas whose composition (Exhibit 2-5) comes from the January 2012 QGESS "Specification for Selected Feedstocks," with methanethiol (mercaptan) added. The gas price is $5.81/GJ ($6.13/MMBtu), HHV basis, delivered to the Midwest, 2011 U.S. dollars (per the November 2012 QGESS fuel price document). Exhibit 2-5 Natural gas composition (volume %): Methane CH4=93.1; Ethane C2H6=3.2; Propane C3H8=0.7; n-Butane C4H10=0.4; Carbon Dioxide CO2=1.0; Nitrogen N2=1.6; Methanethiol CH4S=5.75x10^-6; Total=100.00. Heating values: LHV=47,454 kJ/kg (20,410 Btu/lb) and 34.71 MJ/scm (932 Btu/scf); HHV=52,581 kJ/kg (22,600 Btu/lb) and 38.46 MJ/scm (1,032 Btu/scf). Note A: gas sulfur is mainly the added mercaptan (methanethiol, CH4S) with trace H2S; composition is normalized and heating values are calculated.

Environmental targets are set by two rules: the March 2013 update of the Utility Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) fixes the Hg and hydrochloric acid limits for PC plants, and the February 2013 update of the New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) fixes PM, SO2 and NOx limits for PC and NGCC plants. The rules split coals into low rank and non-low rank by heating value; coal with HHV above 8,300 Btu/lb on a moist, mineral-matter free basis counts as non-low rank, so Illinois No. 6 at 12,900 Btu/lb (moist, mineral-matter free) is non-low rank. Exhibit 2-6 MATS and NSPS emission limits for PM, HCl, SO2, NOx, and Hg (lb/MWh-gross; PC / NGCC): SO2=1.00 / 0.90; NOx=0.70 / 0.43; PM (Filterable)=0.09 / N/A; Hg=3x10^-6 / N/A; HCl=0.010 / N/A. Note A: CO emissions may be added in later revisions if needed.
terms: Utility Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS)

paragraphs.text: These rules cover PC and NGCC units whose construction starts after May 3, 2011, and they define the relevant terms. Fossil fuel means natural gas, oil, coal, or any solid, liquid or gaseous fuel made from them. An electric utility steam generating unit (EGU) is a fossil fuel-fired combustion unit above 25 megawatts electric (MWe) serving a generator that sells electricity; a cogeneration unit also qualifies if it sells to a utility distribution system over 25 MWe and over one-third of the electric output it could potentially produce. A unit is fossil fuel-fired if it can burn more than 25 MW of fossil fuel, meaning those fuels are allowed by its operating permit and suitable fuel handling (coal storage, belts and conveyers, pulverizers, oil storage, etc.) is on site or otherwise available. A coal-fired EGU burns coal for over 10 percent of average annual heat input over any three consecutive calendar years or over 15 percent in any one calendar year. The low-rank virgin coal subcategory covers coal-fired EGUs designed for and burning non-agglomerating virgin coal below 19,305 kJ/kg (8,300 Btu/lb) (moist, mineral matter-free) built and run at or near the producing mine; every other coal-fired EGU falls in the coal ≥8,300 Btu/lb subcategory.

Emission limits for a new plant can also be shaped by the New Source Review (NSR) permitting process and Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD). Under NSR, new sources must install control technology meeting BACT determinations in areas that meet ambient air quality standards (attainment areas) or Lowest Achievable Emission Rate (LAER) technology in areas that do not (non-attainment areas). Area designations vary by county and depend on the exact site; because the EPA Green Book Non-attainment Area Map shows few non-attainment areas in the Midwestern U.S., the study site is taken to be in an attainment area. State and local authorities may impose stricter rules, and since each plant's environmental requirements are unique, some judgment was used in setting the targets.

Exhibit 2-7 Environmental targets for PC cases (pollutant: limit, lb/MWh-gross; control technology). SO2: 1.00; Wet limestone scrubber. NOx: 0.70; Low NOx burners, overfire air and SCR. PM (Filterable): 0.09; Fabric filter. Hg: 3x10^-6; Co-benefit capture, dry sorbent injection, activated carbon injection. HCl: 0.010; SO2 surrogate. Note A: dry sorbent injection holds down SO3 levels and their harmful effect on activated carbon injection (see Section 3.1.6). Note B: SO2 may serve as a surrogate for HCl measurement when the EGU has wet FGD.

For the PC cases, low NOx burners (LNB) with staged overfire air (OFA) are assumed to hold NOx to 0.5 lb/MMBtu and the selective catalytic reduction (SCR) unit to be 83-85 percent efficient, with the SCR ammonia flow trimmed so the NOx limit is met exactly. The wet limestone scrubber is taken as 98 percent efficient, giving SO2 below the NSPS limit; wet flue gas desulfurization (FGD) can now exceed 99 percent removal, but NSPS does not demand it. The fabric filter can exceed 99.9 percent efficiency; since about 99.9 percent was needed in each case, its efficiency was adjusted to hit the PM limit exactly. Meeting the mercury limit needs about 97 percent removal, which the FGD, fabric filter, SCR, activated carbon injection (ACI) and dry sorbent injection (DSI) together are assumed to deliver exactly. DSI is needed because the study coal's high sulfur produces SO3 that would impair Hg capture; Section 3.1.6 covers mercury removal in detail.

Exhibit 2-8 Environmental targets for NGCC cases (pollutant: limit, lb/MWh-gross; control technology). SO2: 0.90; Low sulfur content fuel. NOx: 0.43; Dry low NOx burners and SCR. PM (Filterable): N/A; N/A. Hg: N/A; N/A. HCl: N/A; N/A.

The NGCC plants target roughly 1.0 ppmvd NOx (at 15 percent O2) by combining a dry low NOx (DLN) burner in the CTG, which cuts emissions to about 9 ppmvd (taken as roughly 98 percent NO, at 15 percent O2), with an SCR. A state-of-the-art 2013 F-class CT by itself would already be under the Exhibit 2-8 NOx limit, but an SCR is added so the plant satisfies EPA's prevention of significant deterioration (PSD) program through best available control technology (BACT); it is designed for 90 percent NO reduction on natural gas. Contract terms and industry practice usually cap natural gas total sulfur at 0.25 to 1.00 gr/100 scf, averaging 0.34 gr/100 scf; the study uses that average (4.71x10^-4 lb-S/MMBtu) and treats the added mercaptan (CH4S) as the only sulfur source, at 5.75x10^-6 mol% (7.06x10^-4 lb-CH4S/MMBtu) per Exhibit 2-5. At 1.00 gr-S/100 scf the non-capture SO2 emissions would be 0.018 lb/MWh-gross, and the capture system strips virtually all SO2 from the flue gas. Pipeline gas is assumed free of PM, Hg and HCl, so these emissions are zero.

EPA proposed a CO2 new source performance standard for new fossil fuel-fired electric utility generating units on April 13, 2012, and at publication was finalizing a rule that could set CO2 limits below the emissions of such units lacking CO2 capture. Both PC and NGCC cases assume all combusted fuel carbon becomes CO2 in the flue gas; further CO2 comes from limestone in the FGD system and from activated carbon added for mercury removal. The capture plant is designed to remove 90 percent of the CO2 leaving the FGD system, which yields emissions of 180 - 190 lb/MWh gross for PC and 82 lb/MWh gross for NGCC.

Availability means the share of time in a given period during which a unit can generate. The study assumes each new plant is dispatched whenever available and can produce nameplate capacity while online, so its capacity factor (CF) equals its availability. The period chosen also matters: CF and availability are held constant over plant life in the calculations, although a real plant might need higher peak availability to make up for lower availability in its first several years.

The North American Electric Reliability Council (NERC) Generating Availability Data System (GADS) supplies information on operating plants (e.g. Generating Analysis Reports, Generating Availability Reports, Generating Unit Statistical Brochure, Historical Availability Statistics), including average availability and capacity factor data for coal (e.g. PC) plants by fuel type and capacity. Of the many characteristics in GADS, three are used here to judge existing plant availability and capacity factor: availability factor (AF), net capacity factor (NCF) and equivalent availability factor (EAF).

NCF = NAG / (PH * ((GMC − CU) / Aux)) (net capacity factor = net actual generation divided by active hours times the capacity term formed from gross maximum capacity less station-service capacity over auxiliaries), where NAG is net actual generation, PH the hours the unit spent in the active state, GMC the gross maximum capacity, CU capacity consumed by unit station service and Aux auxiliaries. AF = (PH − (POH + FOH + MOH)) / PH (availability factor = fraction of active hours not lost to planned, forced and maintenance outages), with POH planned outage hours, FOH forced outage hours and MOH maintenance outage hours. EAF = ((PH − (POH + FOH + MOH)) − (EUDH + EPDH + ESEDH)) / PH (equivalent availability factor = available hours less equivalent derated hours, divided by active hours), where EUDH, EPDH and ESEDH are, respectively, the equivalent un-planned, planned and seasonal derated hours. EAF is in effect a measure of plant CF under the assumption that demand for output always exists, since it counts planned, scheduled and seasonal derated hours; it therefore corresponds to the CF definition used in this report.

paragraphs.section: 2.5.3 Capacity Factor for Coal Units without Carbon Capture
paragraphs.text: GADS availability and capacity factor data for coal units in 2011 are given in Exhibit 2-9; to show the trend over time, Exhibit 2-10 gives the same metrics averaged for 2007-2011, and Exhibit 2-11 lists how many generating units are in the 2011 data. Exhibit 2-9 Coal plant availability and capacity factor data for units reporting in 2011 (bar chart of Availability Factor, Net Capacity Factor and Equivalent Availability Factor, %, by coal plant nameplate capacity class from 1-99 MW to 1000 Plus MW; Source: NETL).

paragraphs.section: 2.5.3 Capacity Factor for Coal Units without Carbon Capture
paragraphs.text: Exhibit 2-10 Coal plant availability and CF average data over the period 2007-2011 (Source: NETL) and Exhibit 2-11 Number of coal units included in the 2011 data (Source: NETL) are charts accompanying the GADS review. Against the study's 550 MW net unit size, coal plants of 400-599 MW had an average EAF of 83.7 percent in 2011 and 81.8 percent over 2007-2011, while their average net capacity factor was under 70 percent, a result of demand and dispatch patterns rather than capability.

paragraphs.section: 2.5.3 Capacity Factor for Coal Units without Carbon Capture
paragraphs.text: Although the report assumes dispatch whenever a unit is available, the authors look at how well coal units actually reach high capacity factors using unit-level data from the Ventyx Velocity Suite database. Exhibit 2-12 Number of coal units reporting capacity factors greater than 80% (each year 2000 through 2012; Source: NETL). The peak in 2006-2007 follows U.S. coal electricity demand, which EIA generation data in Exhibit 2-13 U. S. coal electricity power generation (Source: NETL) show topping out in 2007. GADS gives average coal unit availability above 80 percent, and Ventyx Velocity shows as many as 162 coal units running above 85 percent capacity factor in a single year. Because the cost basis is mature plant technology, an 85 percent capacity factor is chosen for the PC units after reviewing these data.

paragraphs.section: 2.5.4 Capacity Factor for Natural Gas Combined Cycle (NGCC) Plants
paragraphs.text: Comparable data were checked for combined cycle plants. In GADS, 160 combined cycle plants averaged 87.8 percent availability in 2011, availability has been around ~ 90 percent every year for the past decade, and it ranged from 80-90 percent on average between 1980 and 1995. An 85 percent capacity factor is therefore adopted for the NGCC plants.

paragraphs.section: 2.5.5 Capacity Factor for Plants with Carbon Capture
paragraphs.text: Carbon capture brings additional equipment, and early reliability studies indicate only a slight drop in reliability when base plant component reliability is unchanged. Both PC and NGCC configurations use a solvent-based capture technology, and capture and CO2 compression both have commercial operating records showing high reliability. Since these are commercial technologies, though deployed at smaller scale, the capacity factor is taken to be the same with or without capture, i.e. 85 percent for PC and NGCC capture plants. For comparison, the EIA Annual Energy Outlook 2013 projected capacity factors for new advanced coal units of 85 percent with capture and 87 percent without.

Unit-level statistics and reported operating experience indicate the selected availability factors are attainable, provided the plant has a quality design incorporating lessons from similar plants, attention to life cycle costs, smart predictive maintenance, trained staff and economic demand for its power; Richwine reports an example of such lessons yielding high availability. Availability depends on the technology, on capital invested (for example, how the design limits scheduled and unplanned maintenance), on maintenance needs and on what the 'customer' requires, such as the cost of a unit being unavailable. Because unavailability costs fall while maintenance and capital costs rise as availability increases, an optimum economic unit availability exists for each application; the study assumes design, maintenance and demand are all consistent with the chosen value.

How individual plant availability changes over plant life has not been analyzed. The study applies a constant 85 percent every year while recognizing that real availability varies year to year; existing data show coal plants can be designed and run at annual availability of 85-100 percent. Plants in this study are expected to sit above and below the selected value in individual years, with the selected value being their effective, levelized availability over the plant life.

Each case received a water balance covering the main water users. Total demand per subsystem was found, and internally recycled water, from sources such as boiler feedwater (BFW) blowdown and, in CO2 capture cases, flue gas condensate, was credited against it; demand minus recycle is raw water withdrawal, i.e. water drawn from the ground or diverted from a municipal supply for plant use. Raw water consumption is the part of the withdrawal that is evaporated, transpired, built into products or otherwise not returned to its source. Half the makeup is assumed to come from groundwater and half from a publicly owned treatment works (POTW). Withdrawal is defined as metered raw water used for any plant purpose, e.g. makeup for the cooling tower, BFW, ash handling and FGD system, and consumption, being withdrawal minus process water returned to the source, expresses the net effect on that source.

BFW blowdown and part of the sour water stripper blowdown are assumed treated and recycled to the cooling tower, while cooling tower blowdown and the remaining SWS blowdown are treated and 90 percent returned to the source, the rest going to ash ponds to evaporate. Cooling tower makeup is the biggest raw water user in every case. All cases use a mechanical draft, evaporative cooling tower, with all process blowdown streams treated and recycled to it. A design wet bulb of 11°C (51.5°F) (Exhibit 2-1 and Exhibit 2-2) and a 5°C (8.5°F) approach give 16°C (60°F) cooling water, and the cooling water range is 11°C (20°F). Makeup is computed from evaporative losses of 0.8 percent of circulating water flow per 10°F of range, drift losses of 0.001 percent of circulating flow, and blowdown losses (BDL) from the equation below.

BDL = EL / (CC − 1) (blowdown losses = evaporative losses divided by cycles of concentration minus one), where EL is evaporative losses and CC is cycles of concentration. Cycles of concentration indicate water quality, and a mid-range value of four (4) is used. The water balances in the case chapters list the demand of the major consumers, the internal recycle supplied, raw water withdrawal (by difference), process water returned to the source, and raw water consumption (also by difference).

Fuller treatment of contracting strategy, EPC contractor services, capital cost contingencies, owner's costs, estimate scope, economic assumptions, finance structures and cost of electricity is given in the April 2011 QGESS "Cost Estimation Methodology for NETL Assessment of Power Plant Performance," parts of which are restated here. The section then repeats the cost caveats from the Executive Summary: estimates carry -15%/+30% uncertainty consistent with AACE Class 4 (feasibility study) estimates for the level of design performed, represent the next commercial offering using vendor cost estimates, and include subsystem process contingencies for expected but undefined costs (difficult for emerging technologies). Fully mature, widely deployed designs (e.g., PC and NGCC without CO2 capture) are costed as nth-of-a-kind (NOAK), having become cheaper through "learning by doing," serial-deployment risk reduction and R&D. Designs with immature technology (e.g., any CO2 capture plant) use the same method, which omits the special premiums of first complex integrations, so early capture plants may cost more. Project- and site-specific factors (contracting strategy, local labor, seismic conditions, water quality, financing, local environmental concerns, weather delays, etc.) can push real costs higher and are outside the stated uncertainty, while ongoing RD&D should produce more advanced, lower-cost designs.

Capital cost is defined at five levels (Exhibit 2-14): BEC, EPCC, TPC, TOC and TASC. The first four are "overnight" costs in "base-year" dollars, the base year being the first year of capital spending; TASC is in mixed, current-year dollars spread across the capital expenditure period, which most NETL studies take as five years when the plant burns coal and three years when it burns natural gas. Bare Erected Cost (BEC) covers process equipment, on-site supporting facilities and infrastructure (e.g., shops, offices, labs, road) and the labor, direct as well as indirect, needed to build or install them, excluding EPC services and contingencies. Engineering, Procurement and Construction Cost (EPCC) is BEC plus EPC contractor services: detailed design, contractor permitting (permits individual contractors need for their scope, not project permitting, which is excluded) and project/construction management. Total Plant Cost (TPC) is EPCC plus project and process contingencies. Total Overnight Cost (TOC) adds owner's costs and every other overnight cost to TPC, with no escalation or interest during construction. Total As-Spent Cost (TASC) totals all capital spending as incurred over the expenditure period, including escalation and interest during construction, and so is in mixed, current-year dollars.

Exhibit 2-14 Capital cost levels and their elements (Source: NETL): a stacked diagram in which process equipment, supporting facilities and direct and indirect labor make up Bare Erected Cost (BEC); adding EPC contractor services gives Engineering, Procurement and Construction Cost (EPCC); adding process contingency and project contingency gives Total Plant Cost (TPC); adding pre-production costs, inventory capital, financing costs and other owner's costs gives Total Overnight Cost (TOC); and adding escalation during the capital expenditure period and interest on debt during the capital expenditure period gives Total As-Spent Cost (TASC). The exhibit notes that BEC, EPCC, TPC and TOC are overnight costs in base-year dollars, whereas TASC is in mixed-year current dollars spread over the capital expenditure period.

Cost estimate basis and classification (2.7.1.1): WorleyParsons estimated TPC and Operation and Maintenance (O&M) costs for every case with its in-house database and conceptual estimating models, calibrated with adjusted vendor-supplied data and actual costs from recent design projects. System code-of-accounts (2.7.1.2): costs are grouped by a process/system oriented code of accounts, which keeps all reasonably allocable parts of a system within that system's account, unlike a facility, area or commodity structure. Estimate scope (2.7.1.3): each estimate is for a complete plant on a generic site, bounded by the "fence line" and including coal receiving and the water supply system, and ending where the main power transformers connect on their high voltage side. T&S cost is kept out of capital and O&M costs and is instead added to the COE.

Capital cost assumptions (2.7.1.4): WorleyParsons' technology-specific conceptual models, built on a reference bottom-up estimate for each major component and maintained from its commercial power and process project experience, produced the capital estimates. Labor is Midwest, Merit Shop: the models are based on the U.S. Gulf Coast and factored to the Midwest using the annual PAS, Inc. (PAS) "Merit Shop Wage & Benefit Survey," applying a payroll-plus-fringe rate weighted over a standard craft mix, for PAS Region 5 (IL, IN, MI, MN, OH, and WI) out of eight regions. Bidding is assumed competitive with enough skilled craft labor locally, on a 50-hour work-week (5-10s) without per-diem or bonus incentives, although such incentives might later be needed depending on competing regional work and craft availability. The site is greenfield, Seismic Zone 1, fairly level, free of hazardous materials, archeological artifacts or excessive rock, with soil good enough for spread footing foundations and no piling. Engineering and Construction Management is 8-10 percent of BEC, covering home office engineering and procurement plus field construction management (a construction manager, resident engineer and scheduler plus staff for field inspection, site safety, materials management, document control and project controls).

Price fluctuations (2.7.1.5): equipment and bulk material prices varied considerably during the work, and reference quotes came from both before and after the 2011 cost year; all vendor quotes were brought to June 2011 dollars using indices such as the Chemical Engineering Plant Cost Index and the Gross Domestic Product Chain-type Price Index. These broad indices are almost flat, but individual equipment types may still diverge from the June 2011 reference. Cross-comparisons (2.7.1.6): in technology comparisons relative cost differences usually matter more than absolute TPC, so a cross-account comparison between technologies was made to check that they move consistently; each item's technical parameters, which drive its cost, must be referenced, and differences in scope or assumptions readily explain apparent anomalies.
terms: Gross Domestic Product Chain-type Price Index

paragraphs.text: Process contingency (2.7.1.6.1) is applied as follows: 20 percent on the Cansolv System in all PC/NGCC capture cases, because post-combustion capture is unproven at commercial scale in power plants, and 5 percent on Instrumentation and Controls in the PC and NGCC capture cases for integration issues. Owner's costs (2.7.1.7): rail spur and switch yard costs are examples of "other" owner's costs; rail spur applies only to PC cases while switch yard applies to all. Switch yard cost depends on voltage, configuration, number of breakers, layout and air- versus gas-insulated design, with a rule of thumb of roughly $850,000 per breaker for a 345 kV air-insulated, ring bus switchyard. On-site rail only (no long runs) is about $850,000 to $950,000 per mi on fairly flat terrain, plus about $50,000 per switch/turnout and about $300 per lineal foot of road crossing. More detail is in the April 2011 QGESS cost estimation methodology.

O&M costs are the production or operating charges and associated maintenance over the plant's expected life, comprising fuel; consumables; operating labor; administrative and support labor; maintenance material and labor; waste disposal; and co-product or by-product credit (a negative cost for by-products sold). They split into fixed O&M, independent of generation, and variable O&M, proportional to generation; taxes and insurance are fixed O&M totaling 2 percent of the TPC. Operating labor (2.7.2.1) is based on the number of operators each case needs, at an average base rate of $39.70/hour with a labor burden of 30 percent of the base rate. Maintenance material and labor (2.7.2.2) follow weighted relationships between maintenance cost and initial capital cost for each major component or section. Administrative and support labor (2.7.2.3) is charged at 25 percent of burdened O&M labor.

Consumables (2.7.2.4), fuel included, are costed from consumption rate, unit cost of each commodity and annual operating hours. Major quantities such as fuel and sorbent come from each plant's heat and mass balance diagrams, and minor ones from reference data. Initial fills and daily consumables are computed at 100 percent operating capacity, and the annual daily-consumable cost is then scaled to the annual operating basis, the CF. Initial fills of consumables, fuels and chemicals are distinct from initial chemical loadings, which sit within equipment pricing in capital cost. Waste disposal (2.7.2.5) is evaluated the same way; PC fly ash and bottom ash are treated as waste at $27.80/tonne ($25.11/ton).

Co-products and by-products (2.7.2.6) are quantified like consumables, but because the market for gypsum and sulfur is uncertain no credit is taken for their sale value. By-product credits or disposal costs may still sway some companies' technology or site choices, and a high local product value can justify extra capital to make a co-product. Ash can be sold in some markets, but activated carbon injection in the PC cases may make the fly ash unmarketable, so ash is treated as a waste with a disposal cost.

T&S cost for CO2 in a deep saline formation is estimated with the FE/NETL CO2 Transport Cost Model and the FE/NETL CO2 Saline Storage Cost Model (detailed in the May 2014 QGESS "Carbon Dioxide Transport and Storage Costs in NETL Studies"). Costs are given as first-year values in $/tonne of CO2 that rise at a nominal 3 percent per year, the general inflation rate used in NETL studies, and are in 2011 dollars. For the CO2 source they act as a disposal cost per tonne captured over an assumed 30-year operating period; for the pipeline and storage operator they are the first-year break-even price needed over those 30 years to recover all costs and earn the required internal rate of return on equity (IRROE).
terms: FE/NETL CO2 Saline Storage Cost Model
internal rate of return on equity (IRROE)

paragraphs.text: The Transport Cost Model estimates building and running a dedicated CO2 pipeline from source to storage site, buried at shallow depth so the CO2 is at soil temperature, usually about 50 °F. CO2 enters at the plant gate at 2,200 psig and leaves at the storage site at 1,200 psig, pressures at which CO2 is liquid between roughly -64°F and 88°F. The pipeline is 100 km (62.1 mi) long and carries an average 3.2 million tonnes of CO2 a year (about 8,770 tonnes per day); designed for 80 percent of maximum mass flow, its maximum design rate is about 10,960 tonnes/day. The model finds the smallest standard pipe diameter that can carry this flow the full distance without boosting, and also the smallest diameter when boost pumps at equal spacing raise pressure from 1,200 psig back to 2,200 psig, then selects the cheapest option (no boost pump, one, two, three, etc.). Its capital and operating costs come from open literature, with pipeline capital based on Oil and Gas Journal natural gas pipeline costs adjusted for the higher CO2 pipeline pressure.

Financial inputs of the FE/NETL CO2 Transport Cost Model: debt to equity ratio 50%/50%; nominal interest rate on debt 4.5%/year; nominal IRROE 12%; escalation rate 3%; tax rate 38%; project contingency factor 15%. Using a weighted average cost of capital approach, the model computes the first-year break-even transport price covering all costs plus the minimum return on equity, which from the source's standpoint is also the minimum transport cost; it comes to $2.24/tonne in 2011 dollars.

The FE/NETL CO2 Saline Storage Cost Model gives detailed costs for CO2 injection and monitoring under EPA rules for Class VI injection wells and for monitoring and reporting under Subpart RR of the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Rule. Cost depends strongly on financial inputs, the timeline of each storage stage and the activities within it. Financial inputs: debt to equity ratio 45%/55%; nominal interest on debt 5.5%/year; nominal IRROE 12%; escalation 3%; financial responsibility for post-injection site care and site closure met by pre-funding a modified trust fund during injection; project contingency factor 15% and process contingency factor 20%. The six stages are: regional evaluation and initial site selection, 1 year; site characterization, 3 years, in which four sites are characterized, one successful site is chosen and pore space rights are leased; permitting, 2 years, with injection wells drilled, tested and completed; operations, 30 years, installing buildings, surface equipment, monitoring wells and equipment, meeting permit conditions and funding the trust; post-injection site care and site closure, 50 years, continuing monitoring, verification and accounting (MVA) paid from the operator's trust fund; and long-term stewardship, not modeled explicitly but represented by a state-sponsored trust fund the operator pays into during operations.

Since saline formation geology differs across the U.S., storage and monitoring costs are made region-specific to match the plant locations used in NETL techno-economic studies, by pairing four generic locations with candidate basins: Midwest with the Illinois Basin, Texas with the East Texas Basin, North Dakota with the Williston Basin and Montana with the Powder River Basin. A storage supply-cost curve was built for each basin, and the cost at 25 gigatonnes (Gt) of storage potential (Exhibit 2-15) is used; this is conservative because decades or more than a century would pass before any one basin stored 25 Gt, which would serve 125 GW of coal power with 90 percent capture for 30 years. The last column of Exhibit 2-15 gives the T&S cost used for each location, rounded to the nearest dollar; only the $11/tonne Midwest value applies to this volume.

Exhibit 2-15 CO2 transport and storage costs (columns: basin; transport, 2011 $/tonne; storage cost at 25 Gt, 2011 $/tonne; T&S value for system studies, 2011$/tonne). Midwest: Basin=Illinois; Transport=2.24; Storage=8.69; T&S value=11. Texas: Basin=East Texas; Transport=2.24; Storage=8.83; T&S value=11. North Dakota: Basin=Williston; Transport=2.24; Storage=13.95; T&S value=16. Montana: Basin=Powder River; Transport=2.24; Storage=21.81; T&S value=24. Note A: transport plus storage is rounded to the nearest dollar.

paragraphs.section: 2.7.4 Cost of CO2 Captured and Avoided
paragraphs.text: Cost of CO2 Captured = (COE_CCS − COE_NonCCS) / CO2 Captured_CCS (the minimum plant gate CO2 sales price that makes capture preferable to a defined reference non-capture plant: COE increase divided by CO2 captured per MWh). Cost of CO2 Avoided = (COE_CCS with T&S − COE_NonCCS) / (CO2 Emissions_NonCCS − CO2 Emissions_CCS) (the minimum CO2 emissions price, charged to both capture and non-capture plants, that makes capture preferable: COE increase including T&S divided by stack emissions reduction per MWh). CCS is the capture plant evaluated and Non-CCS the reference plant; COE is in $/MWh, the CCS plant includes compression to 2,215 psia, the COE for CO2 Captured excludes transportation and storage (T&S) and the COE for CO2 Avoided includes T&S; CO2 Captured and CO2 Emissions (stack) are in tonne/MWh. For greenfield coal plants with CCS, the reference is a non-capture plant of the supercritical pulverized coal (SCPC) type; for greenfield natural gas systems, the reference is a non-capture natural gas plant.

Chapter 3 reports four PC-fired Rankine cycle plant designs, each built on market-ready technology assumed to be commercially available by plant startup and each using a one-on-one arrangement of a state-of-the art PC steam generator burning Illinois No. 6 coal with a single steam turbine. With and without CO2 capture, all are compared at a common 550 MWe net; the capture designs have bigger gross units to cover larger auxiliary loads. A constant net output gives a meaningful side-by-side comparison, and is feasible because boiler and steam turbine suppliers have shown commercially that they can size units to a custom specification.

Steam conditions came from canvassing original equipment manufacturers (OEM) of boilers and steam turbines, who were asked which most advanced conditions they would guarantee for a U.S. commercial subcritical or SC PC unit of nominal 550 MWe net firing Illinois No. 6. On that basis the single-reheat conditions are 16.5 MPa/566°C/566°C (2,400 psig/1,050°F/1,050°F) for the subcritical cases (B11A and B11B) and 24.1 MPa/593°C/593°C (3,500 psig/1,100°F/1,100°F) for the SC cases (B12A and B12B). Allowable steam temperature depends on how corrosive the fuel is: most OEMs felt such conditions would be confined to low sulfur coal (e.g. PRB), because running hotter on high sulfur coal like Illinois No. 6 would raise coal ash corrosion wastage of the hottest superheater and reheater (RH) sections exponentially, forcing pressure part replacement outages about every 10 or 15 years and cancelling the fuel and emissions savings of higher efficiency. Three of the newest SC units in North America use similar cycles: the James E. Rogers Energy Complex in North Carolina, started in 2012 (27.0 MPa/568°C/579°C [3,922 psia/1,055°F/1,075°F]), and Prairie State Energy Campus units 1 and 2, also started in 2012 (26.2 MPa/568°C/568°C [3,800 psig/1,055°F/1,055°F]). Section 2 gives site ambient conditions, fuel composition and the emissions control basis.

Several process areas recur in every PC configuration, for example coal receiving and storage, emissions control and power generation. To avoid repeating long descriptions in each case section, Section 3.1 describes them once as background, and the case sections then give their performance.

paragraphs.section: 3.1.1 Coal, Activated Carbon, and Sorbent Receiving and Storage
paragraphs.text: The Coal Receiving and Storage system unloads, conveys, prepares and stores delivered coal, from the trestle bottom dumper and coal receiving hoppers through to the slide gate valves at the coal storage silo outlets. It is sized to run for 16 hours at the 5 percent over pressure/valves wide open (OP/VWO) condition and for long-term operation of 90 days or more at maximum continuous rating (MCR). The sorbent receiving and storage system covers the day storage bin, conveyors, unloading hoppers, truck roadways and turnarounds. Coal arrives in 100-car unit trains of 91 tonne (100 ton) rail cars, which the trestle bottom dumper empties into two receiving hoppers, each feeding a vibratory feeder that drops 8 cm x 0 (3" x 0) coal onto a belt conveyor. Two conveyors and an intermediate transfer tower bring the coal to the stacker, which sends it to the long-term storage pile or the reclaim area, passing a magnetic plate separator that removes tramp iron. Two vibratory feeders under the reclaim pile load a belt conveyor to the coal surge bin in the crusher tower, where crushers reduce the coal to 2.5 cm x 0 (1" x 0); it is then conveyed to the transfer tower, where a tripper fills one of six boiler silos.

paragraphs.section: 3.1.1 Coal, Activated Carbon, and Sorbent Receiving and Storage
paragraphs.text: Limestone comes in 23 tonne (25 ton) trucks that tip into a below grade hopper; a feeder passes it to a conveyor and the storage pile, and from there it is reclaimed via a hopper to a day bin. Powdered activated carbon (PAC), non-halogenated, arrives in 18 tonne (20 ton) trucks that unload pneumatically into a storage silo; a feeder hopper delivers it to a screw feeder and drop tube, which feeds the eductor suction port, from where it is piped and injected through lances spread across the flue gas duct upstream of the baghouse. Hydrated lime is handled almost identically: it is held in a main storage silo and passed to a weigh hopper, then piped to the sorbent distribution manifold located ahead of the air preheater.

The subcritical PC steam generator is a wall-fired drum-type unit with natural circulation and balanced draft, having a totally enclosed dry bottom furnace, superheater, reheater, economizer and air preheater. The SC steam generator is a wall-fired, balanced draft Benson-boiler of the once-through, spiral-wound kind with a water-cooled dry bottom furnace and likewise has a superheater, reheater, economizer and air preheater. In both, combustion uses LNBs and OFA. The plant is assumed designed for base-load service but with some allowance for daily or weekly cycling.

Scope (3.1.2.1): the steam generator for both subcritical and SC PC units comprises a drum-type evaporator (subcritical only) or once-through type steam generator (SC only); a startup circuit with integral separators (SC only); a water-cooled, dry bottom furnace; a two-stage superheater; a reheater (RH); an economizer; a spray type desuperheater; a soot blower system; air preheaters (Ljungstrom type); coal feeders and pulverizers; low NOx coal burners with light oil igniters/warm-up system; an OFA system; forced draft (FD) fans; primary air (PA) fans; and induced draft (ID) fans.

Feedwater and steam, subcritical (3.1.2.2): feedwater (FW) picks up heat from the leaving combustion gases in the economizer, goes to the boiler drum and is distributed to the water wall circuits around the furnace. After the lower and upper furnace circuits and the steam drum, steam flows via the convection enclosure circuits into the primary superheater and then the secondary superheater and leaves for the high pressure (HP) turbine. HP turbine exhaust comes back to the steam generator as cold reheat and goes on to the intermediate pressure (IP) turbine as hot reheat.

Feedwater and steam, SC: FW enters the economizer bottom header, rises through the economizer tube bank and the stringer tubes that carry the primary superheater, and collects in the economizer outlet headers, from which external downcomers take it to the furnace hopper inlet headers. It then rises through the furnace hopper and wall tubes to the steam water separator. Below the Benson point (low load) the separator water is sent back to the economizer inlet by the boiler recirculating pump; above it the unit runs once through. Steam goes from the separator via the furnace roof to the convection pass enclosure walls and primary superheater, through the first water attemperation stage to the furnace platens, through the second attemperation stage to the intermediate superheater, and then to the final superheater and outlet pipe terminal; the two spray attemperation stages hold temperatures tightly in all hot sections during fast load changes. Reheat steam from the turbine crosses the primary reheater, then crossover piping with inter-stage attemperation (for outlet temperature control during load changes) feeding the final reheater banks and back to the turbine.

Air and combustion products (3.1.2.3): FD fan air is heated in Ljungstrom air preheaters by the boiler exhaust gas and supplied to the burner windbox as secondary air. PA fans provide air to carry PC to the burners; it is also preheated in the Ljungstrom units to dry the coal, while some PA fan air bypasses the preheaters to regulate the coal/air temperature leaving the mills. The PC-air mixture enters coal nozzles at several furnace elevations; hot gases rise through the superheater and reheater sections, then the economizer and air preheater, and leave the steam generator, passing in turn the SCR reactor, the manifolds for dry sorbent injection (DSI) and then activated carbon injection (ACI), the fabric filter and ID fan, and finally the FGD system before the stack. Fuel feed (3.1.2.4): crushed Illinois No. 6 bituminous coal is fed to each mill (one of the pulverizers) and ground to about 72 percent passing 200 mesh with under 0.5 percent retained on 50 mesh, then carried by PA fan air through coal piping to the furnace wall nozzles.

Ash removal (3.1.2.5): the furnace bottom has several refractory-lined welded steel hoppers, each with a clinker grinder, and a water-filled seal trough around the upper edge for cooling and sealing. Water and ash go through the clinker grinder to an ash sluice system and on to hydrobins for dewatering before trucking offsite (the rest of the bottom ash system is in Section 3.1.11); fly ash hoppers are placed beneath both the air preheater and economizer outlets. Burners (3.1.2.6): a boiler of this size has roughly 24 to 36 coal nozzles at several elevations, each a low-NOx design that stages combustion, with OFA nozzles staging it further; each burner has an oil-fired pilot torch used to light, warm up and hold a stable flame during startup and at low loads. DSI (3.1.2.7): the hydrated lime injection manifold for SO3 control sits just ahead of the air preheaters (see Section 3.1.6). Air preheaters (3.1.2.8): two vertical-shaft Ljungstrom regenerative units driven by electric motors through gear reducers. Soot blowers (3.1.2.9): 50 to 150 retractable nozzles and lances blast furnace walls and convection surfaces with HP steam, sequenced to suit coal quality and surface design and driven by electric motors.

The PC plants are designed for the 0.70 lb/MWh-gross NOx target using two steps. First, LNBs plus staged OFA in the boiler lower NOx to about 0.5 lb/MMBtu. Second, an SCR system upstream of the air heater uses ammonia and a catalyst to convert NOx to N2 and H2O; it has three subsystems (reactor vessel, ammonia storage and injection, gas flow control) and its design target is 83-85 percent reduction while allowing 2 ppmv ammonia slip when the catalyst reaches end of life. SCR capital cost, including the first catalyst charge, is carried within the boiler cost. Selective non-catalytic reduction (SNCR) was considered but rejected: after LNBs and OFA the remaining NOx is fairly low, which makes reaching the limit with SNCR hard, since SNCR suits medium to high NOx levels needing 40 to 60 percent removal, whereas the catalyst lets SCR achieve higher efficiencies at low NOx concentrations.

SCR operation (3.1.3.1): the reactor vessel is sized to give the ammonia, injected just before the vessel, enough residence time with the NOx in the boiler exhaust, and the catalyst inside promotes their reaction. Catalyst active materials include titanium dioxide, vanadium pentoxide and tungsten trioxide, and vanadium/titanium catalysts operate between 260°C (500°F) and 455°C (850°F). An economizer bypass supplies flue gas at the needed temperature during low flow such as low load, and soot-blowing equipment cleans the catalyst. Ammonia storage and injection comprises unloading facilities, a bulk storage tank, vaporizers, a dilution air skid and an injection grid. Flue gas flow control comprises the ductwork, dampers and flow straightening devices routing boiler exhaust to the SCR reactor and then the air heater, plus the economizer bypass and its dampers for low-load temperature control.
The PAC injection manifold sits just upstream of the baghouse; the system is described fully in Section 3.1.6.

The fabric filter (baghouse) has two separate single-stage, in-line, multi-compartment units of high air-to-cloth ratio (0.9-1.5 m/min [3-5 ft/min]) with pulse-jet on-line cleaning. Ash gathers on the outside of bags held on steel cages and the dust cake is knocked off by compressed air pulses. Bags are polyphenylensulfide (PPS) with intrinsic Teflon Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) coating, rated 180°C (356°F) continuous and 210°C (410°F) peak. Each compartment has filter bag gas passages and heated ash hoppers inside a rigid steel casing, with control devices, inlet gas distribution, insulators, nozzles, expansion joints and similar items. ACI and DSI raise fly ash calcium content and filter loading, increasing total particulate by about 26 percent, though calcium is not expected to raise trace metal leaching appreciably. Class F fly ash (from bituminous coal) is sometimes sold as concrete filler, but less commonly than high-calcium Class C fly ash, which is more valuable as a Portland cement substitute; Class F fly ash needs low unburned carbon, and the activated carbon and hydrated lime (really the CaSO4 product) would make this fly ash unsuitable for concrete.

Part of the mercury removal comes from flue gas reactions of mercury with available halogens and carbon (a footnote says much of this section's text and images come, with permission, from an ADA-ES quote to NETL for an ADA-ES mercury control system). Coal halogens, mainly chlorine, set how much mercury is oxidized across the SCR and air preheater, and so affect removal in fabric filters and wet scrubbers; chlorine above 500 ppmv seems to add nothing further to the oxidation rate. An SCR can change the SO3 or H2SO4 in the flue gas, and sulfuric acid can hinder mercury adsorption on unburned carbon. For the PC design basis, unmitigated SO3 at the air preheater inlet is estimated at 59 ppmvd, which would leave both unburned and added activated carbon removing little mercury, so DSI is added to bring SO3 to about 2 ppmvd (Section 3.1.6.1). Higher ammonia, from running the SCR harder for NOx, also lowers the oxidized mercury fraction.

Unburned carbon can both catalyze mercury oxidation and adsorb mercury, and bituminous coal plants usually have enough of it for one or both effects to matter substantially. Unburned and/or activated carbon on the fabric filter surface, together with fairly high hydrogen halides (e.g. HCl), should leave much of the mercury oxidized at the filter outlet; oxidized mercury dissolves in water and is readily caught in the wet scrubber. Depending on scrubber chemistry, some captured mercury can revert to the poorly soluble elemental form and be re-emitted. The control systems chosen keep mercury entering the scrubber low, reducing the chance of exceeding the limit, although stack spikes may still occur if mercury built up in a recirculating scrubber is released; careful operation and the 30- or 90-day averaging period in the rules largely limit their effect on compliance.

EPA estimated Hg co-benefit capture statistically with a "best demonstrated technology" approach, a fabric filter plus FGD for bituminous coal, giving 86.7 percent with a range of 83.8 to 98.8 percent. EPA's Integrated Planning Model (IPM) documentation lists mercury emission modification factors (EMF), equal to one minus removal efficiency, for 190 boiler/control combinations; for PC boilers (not cyclones, stokers, fluidized beds or 'others') with fabric filter, SCR and wet FGD the EMF is 0.1, i.e. 90 percent removal, while EPA Information Collection Request (ICR) data for U.S. bituminous boilers with fabric filters and wet FGD average 98 percent. Co-benefit capture for SCR + fabric filter + wet FGD is thus bounded between 83.8 and 98 percent, and the study assumes 90 percent, near the mid-point and equal to the IPM value. Because that is not enough to meet the mercury limit, ADA-ES provided a cost and performance estimate specifying ACI and DSI. Placing DSI ahead of the air preheater, instead of downstream where the limit is still assumed attainable, lets the preheater cool the gas further, improving plant performance and raising carbon efficiency by up to 25 percent.

Illinois No. 6 coal has fairly high sulfur (2.82 wt%), and ADA-ES estimates about 36 ppmvd sulfur trioxide (SO3) at the air preheater outlet from combustion and SCR oxidation. SO3 harms the mercury capture of both unburned and activated carbon: in Mercury Research Center tests on an ESP-configured system with 10 lb/MMacf activated carbon injected upstream of the air preheater, mercury removal was below 50 percent when SO3 exceeded 20 ppm, and below 70 and 80 percent when SO3 exceeded 10 and 3 ppm, respectively. Hydrated lime injection upstream of the air preheater was chosen for SO3 control, letting the preheater discharge gas at a lower 290°F and lifting overall plant efficiency compared with no DSI or DSI downstream; without SO3 mitigation the gas leaving the preheater would have to stay above the acid dew point, about 337°F.

DSI and ACI systems are nearly the same, so one description covers both. Per Exhibit 3-1, DSI dilute-phase pneumatically conveys a metered flow of hydrated lime from a bulk silo to the flue gas duct, where it reacts with SO3 to form CaSO4 that the fabric filter captures. Self-unloading pneumatic trucks deliver 40,000 lb batches, blown by an on-board compressor into a dry welded-steel silo whose displaced air exits via a silo vent filter; instrumentation tracks silo level, and compressed-air fluidization valves and nozzles pulse air to keep lime flowing from the chisel-type cone. A rotary valve passes fluidized lime to a feeder hopper, and a screw feeder, whose speed sets the feed rate, drops it via the drop tube into the eductor suction port. Low-pressure blowers supply motive air to the eductors, creating suction that draws lime and air into the mixing zone; the lime is then piped to injection lances designed to spread it across the duct upstream of the air preheater. The distributed control system (DCS) monitors and adjusts the DSI system to demand. Exhibit 3-1 Typical injection process flow diagram (Source: permission granted from ADA-ES).

ADA-ES tested mercury control with ACI plus trona-based DSI on a unit with a fabric filter and high SO3 (greater than 20 ppm) at a flue gas temperature of 380°F; the results (Exhibit 3-2) show high mercury removal is possible when alkaline material is present with activated carbon on the bag surface, and better performance is expected at lower temperature. Exhibit 3-2 Mercury removal across a fabric filter during a high-sulfur bituminous test (Hg removal % versus injection concentration lb/Mmacf, for 380F with 10 to 20 ppm SO3 and 380F with Trona; Source: permission granted from ADA-ES). To meet the mercury limit, PAC is injected at about 2.7 lb/MMacf in every PC case. The ACI injection manifold is located directly upstream of the fabric filter and is otherwise identical to the DSI system of Section 3.1.6.1.

The FGD unit is a non-reheat, positive pressure absorber using wet limestone forced oxidation, producing gypsum and operating with a wet-stack; it scrubs SO2 from boiler exhaust before release or before the Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) facility, at 98 percent sulfur removal in all cases. In capture Cases B11B and B12B, SO2 must be cut further to about 1 ppmv to limit amine heat stable salts (HSS) in CO2 absorption, so the CDR unit has a polishing scrubber taking SO2 from roughly 37 ppmv at FGD exit to the required level ahead of the CDR absorber. FGD scope starts at the ID fan outlet and ends at the stack inlet in Cases B11A and B12A or at the CDR inlet in Cases B11B and B12B, and the description is split into limestone handling and reagent preparation, the FGD scrubber, and byproduct dewatering.

Limestone handling and reagent preparation (3.1.7.1) grinds and slurries delivered limestone, from the day bin to the limestone feed system, for continuous base load duty. Each day bin feeds a 100 percent capacity wet ball mill through a weigh feeder; the mill grinds limestone to 90 to 95 percent passing 325 mesh (44 microns), with water added at the inlet to form limestone slurry that goes to a mill slurry tank. Two mill recycle pumps per tank send it to hydrocyclones and distribution boxes that classify it by solids content and size: underflow carrying oversize returns to the mill, and overflow with correctly sized limestone goes to a reagent storage tank, from which reagent distribution pumps feed the absorber module.

FGD scrubber (3.1.7.2): gas leaving the boiler air preheater goes through one of two parallel fabric filters, the ID fans, and a single 100 percent capacity counter-current absorber. At the bottom it receives an initial quenching spray of reagent and then rises through the spray zone, where several spray levels with headers and nozzles keep reagent concentration even, and then through several levels of moisture separators made of chevron-shaped vanes that strip entrained droplets inertially by forcing sharp turns; the scrubbed gas leaves the top for the stack or the CDR process. Slurry collects in the large liquid inventory at the vessel bottom, where oxidation air turns calcium sulfite into calcium sulfate (gypsum) and continuously running agitators keep solids suspended and mix in the air. Recirculation pumps, with spares, return slurry to the spray levels; fresh reagent makeup and removal of byproduct solids by bleed pumps (also with a spare) hold the chemical equilibrium, with solids sent to dewatering and slurry pH and density monitored.

The FGD runs as a wet stack. Scrubber bypass or reheat, used at some older plants to keep exhaust above saturation temperature, is omitted because modern scrubbers have better mist eliminators and detailed flow modeling of the flue lets gutters and drains be placed to catch and drain any moisture; hence there is no need to heat the exhaust above the 56°C (133°F) FGD discharge temperature.

Byproduct dewatering (3.1.7.3) dewaters FGD bleed slurry into wallboard grade gypsum; its scope begins at the connections on the bleed pump discharge and ends at the pile where gypsum is stored. The circulating reagent continuously gains dissolved and suspended solids from SO2 absorption, so part of it is steadily drawn off by bleed pumps and replaced by fresh reagent from the reagent distribution pumps. Gypsum (calcium sulfate) forms when oxygen is injected into the calcium sulfite in the absorber sump; the bleed holds about 20 wt% gypsum and goes to a primary dewatering hydrocyclone cluster, which thickens it from 20 wt% to 50 wt% solids and separates CaCO3 from CaSO4•2H2O, giving a limestone stoichiometry of 1.10 in the absorber and 1.05 overall and lowering FGD operating cost. Hydrocyclone underflow goes to a filter feed tank and is pumped to a horizontal belt vacuum filter, with two 100 percent filter systems for redundancy.

Hydrocyclones (3.1.7.4) are simple, reliable devices without moving parts that raise slurry concentration to about 50 wt% in one step, as needed for the vacuum belt filter. Feed enters tangentially and spins, so heavy particles move to the wall and exit at the bottom while some lighter particles collect in the center and leave at the top, concentrating the underflow from 20 wt% to 50 wt%. Two hydrocyclone clusters, each with five 15 cm (6 inch) units on a common feed header, handle the absorber bleed, with four cyclones running at design and one spare. Overflow and underflow go to separate launders; the overflow, still about 5 wt% solids of gypsum, fly ash and limestone residue, returns to the absorber, and the underflow goes to the filter feed tank and then the horizontal belt vacuum filters.

Horizontal vacuum belt filters (3.1.7.5) form the secondary dewatering step. The pre-thickened 50 wt% gypsum slurry is pumped into an overflow pan and spreads onto the moving vacuum belt, where a cake forms and is dried to roughly 90 wt% solids by the time it reaches the discharge end. There the filter cloth passes over a roller that releases the cake, which drops down a chute to the pile ahead of final byproduct use. A vacuum pump provides the vacuum; filtrate is held in a filtrate tank as surge for limestone grinding, and any filtrate not used for limestone slurry goes back to the absorber.

In Cases B11B and B12B a CDR facility, together with compressors and a dryer, removes 90 percent of the CO2 in the gas leaving the FGD, purifies it and compresses it to a supercritical state (a footnote says much of this section is based, with permission, on Shell Cansolv data supplied to NETL for its CO2 removal system). The FGD outlet gas carries about 1 percent more CO2 than raw flue gas because limestone releases CO2 in the FGD absorber. Its main parts are a pre-scrubber, a CO2 absorber, an absorbent purification unit and a CO2 stripper. The process follows 2012 Shell Cansolv data (typical flowsheet in Exhibit 3-3) and is intended to recover high-purity CO2 from low pressure (LP), oxygen-containing streams such as coal plant flue gas, CT exhaust and other waste gases.

Pre-scrubber (3.1.8.1): a booster fan pushes FGD outlet gas through the downstream equipment, the first being the pre-scrubber inlet cooling section, where a direct contact cooler saturates the gas and sub-cools it; this raises amine absorption capacity and so lowers amine circulation. Next, caustic scrubbing in the pre-scrubber sulfur polishing section cuts SO2 entering the CO2 absorber to 1 ppmv and halves NO2 (50 percent reduction). CO2 absorber (3.1.8.2): the Cansolv absorber is one rectangular, acid resistant, brick-lined concrete structure filled with stainless-steel packing in four sections, three for CO2 absorption and a top water-wash section; this geometry costs less than conventional columns while matching or bettering their performance. Gas flows counter-current to the Cansolv solvent and about 90 percent of the incoming CO2 is taken up by the lean solvent, the rest passing to the water-wash. Hot amine is drawn off before the bottom packing section, pumped through a heat exchanger for intercooling and to limit water loss, and returned just above the final packing section.

Exhibit 3-3 Cansolv CO2 capture process typical flow diagram (Source: NETL). The top water-wash section strips volatiles and entrained amine from the gas and condenses and keeps water in the system: wash water, a mix of recirculated wash water and water condensed from the flue gas, is drawn from the bottom of the section, pumped through a heat exchanger and returned at the top, and the washed flue gas is then vented to atmosphere.

Amine regeneration (3.1.8.3): rich amine from the absorber bottom is pumped through a rich/lean heat exchanger, a stainless steel plate and frame unit with a 5°C (9°F) approach, where lean amine heats it; a second exchanger can preheat it further using LP steam condensate from the regenerator reboiler or IP steam condensate from amine purification. It enters near the top of the stainless steel stripper, which has structured stainless steel packing. The regenerator reboiler, a stainless steel plate and frame unit with a 3°C (5°F) approach, uses LP steam to make water vapor that rises counter to the falling rich amine and strips CO2. Lean amine from the stripper bottom goes to a flash vessel, where released water vapor is recompressed and sent back to the stripper bottom, then through the rich/lean exchanger to the lean amine tank. Vapor and CO2 rising in the stripper meet recycled reflux that condenses some vapor; the rest is partly condensed in the condenser, and in the reflux accumulator the CO2 product gas is split off and passed at about 30 psia to the CO2 compressor while the water returns as reflux. Reboiler steam is proportional to rich amine flow but also depends on stripper top temperature; at steady state the reboiler alone needs about 1,100 Btu/lb CO2 of LP steam, extracted from the IP-LP crossover pipe of the steam turbine.

Amine purification (3.1.8.4), done in batch in the Cansolv process, removes part of the HSS and the ionic and non-ionic amine degradation products. Ion exchange (3.1.8.4.1): HSS arise from residual NO2 and SO2 in the flue gas; acids from oxidative amine degradation and from reactions with NO2 and SO2 neutralize some amine so it can no longer absorb CO2, and excess HSS are removed in an ion exchange resin bed in a column. Thermal reclaimer (3.1.8.4.2): a slipstream of treated amine from the ion exchanger is distilled under vacuum to separate water and amine, leaving non-ionic degradation products as bottoms that are pumped to storage, diluted and cooled with process water and disposed of; part of the condensed amine and water goes back to the absorber and the rest to the lean amine tank.

The CO2 compression system was modeled from vendor data, with a design similar to that in the Carbon Capture Simulation Initiative's (CCSI) "Centrifugal Compressor Simulation User Manual": an 8-stage front-loaded centrifugal compressor. Exhibit 3-4 CO2 compressor interstage pressures (stage: outlet pressure, MPa (psia); stage pressure ratio). Stage 1: 0.44 (64); 2.23. Stage 2: 0.92 (133); 2.14. Stage 3: 1.72 (250); 1.90. Stage 4: 3.04 (441); 1.78. Stage 5: 4.80 (696); 1.59. Stage 6: 6.97 (1,011); 1.53. Stage 7: 10.36 (1,502); 1.49. Stage 8: 15.27 (2,215); 1.48. Power use was estimated with 89 percent polytropic efficiency and 97 percent mechanical efficiency for stages 1-7 and 91 percent polytropic efficiency for the last stage.

Intercooling is provided for every stage, and the first three stages also have water knockout; there is no aftercooler. A triethylene glycol (TEG) dehydration unit between stages 4 and 5, at 3.03 MPa (439 psia), dries the CO2 to 300 ppmw moisture, designed after a Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) paper on conditioning CO2 from capture for transport and storage. In such an absorption unit wet gas rises through a column against descending TEG, which takes up water by physical absorption because water dissolves in it more readily than the other gas components; dry gas leaves overhead and water-rich solvent leaves at the bottom, is depressurized to about atmospheric, heated and passed through a regeneration column where the water boils off. Depending on configuration, TEG units can achieve below 10 ppm water.

A separate study looked at alternatives to dumping CO2 compression heat to cooling water. Using part of the heat to preheat BFW (the rest still going to cooling water) raised net plant efficiency by 0.3 percentage points (absolute). A second option reworked compression intercooling to drive a LiBr-H2O absorption refrigeration system with water as refrigerant: each single intercooler gave way to a kettle reboiler plus two counter-current exchangers of shell and tube design, the kettle reboiler acting as generator that passes compression heat to the LiBr-H2O solution to separate refrigerant from brine, the second exchanger rejecting heat to cooling water, and the evaporator exchanger cooling the CO2 by vaporizing refrigerant. This Approach 2 needed only five compression stages, with higher ratios so each compressor outlet was at least 93°C (200°F) to keep a 6°C (10°F) gradient in the kettle reboiler, and raised efficiency by only 0.1 percentage points (absolute). Neither small gain was judged worth the extra cost and operating complexity, so neither was adopted in the base design.

The steam turbine is built for long-term (90 days or more) MCR operation with throttle control valves 95 percent open and can run short-term (16 hours) at the 5 percent OP/VWO condition. In the subcritical cases it is a tandem compound HP-IP-two LP (double flow) machine in three casings, for condensing single reheat duty, with non-automatic extractions and four-flow exhaust, driving a hydrogen-cooled generator; it has DC motor-operated lube oil pumps and shaft-driven main lube oil pumps. Exhaust pressure is 50.8 cm (2 in) Hg in a single pressure condenser, which is two-shell, transverse, with a divided waterbox per shell, and there are seven extraction points. SC turbine-generators are similar apart from steam conditions and extraction points: both subcritical cases have seven extractions, while the SC capture plant has only 6 and the SC non-capture plant 8 (the B12A/B12B difference is explained in Section 3.1.11).

A pressurized oil system that is closed-loop and water-cooled lubricates the bearings, and shafts are sealed against air in-leakage and steam blowout by labyrinth glands tied to an LP steam seal system. The generator stator is cooled by a skid-mounted CL water system (circulating pumps, shell and tube or plate and frame exchangers, filters, deionizers) and the rotor by hydrogen gas recirculation driven by fans on the rotor shaft. An electro-hydraulic control system operates the stop, control, reheat stop and intercept valves. Main steam enters through the stop and control valves at 16.5 MPa/566°C (2,400 psig/1,050°F) in the subcritical cases and 24.1 MPa/593°C (3,500 psig/1,100°F) in the SC cases, entering near the middle of the HP span and returning to the boiler for reheat; reheat steam passes the reheat stop and intercept valves into the IP section at 566°C (1,050°F) (subcritical) or 593°C (1,100°F) (SC). IP exhaust goes by crossover pipe to the two LP sections, splits into four paths and exhausts downward to the condenser, the last LP stages running as condensing stages with 9.2 to 9.5 percent exit liquid. The turbine is designed for constant inlet steam pressure over the full load range.

Balance of plant covers the condensate and FW systems, the main, reheat and extraction steam systems, ash handling, ducting and stack, and waste treatment plus miscellaneous systems. The condensate system (3.1.11.1) pumps condensate from the condenser hotwell through the LP FW heaters to the deaerator; it has one main condenser, two 50 percent variable speed motor-driven vertical condensate pumps, four LP heaters (two in Case B12B) and a deaerator with storage tank. The pumps discharge through separate lines, each with check and gate valves, into a common header, and a common minimum flow recirculation line back to the condenser downstream of the gland steam condenser protects the minimum flows of that condenser and the pumps. LP heaters 1 through 4 are 50 percent capacity, parallel flow units in the condenser neck; the other FW heaters are 100 percent shell and U-tube exchangers. Each LP heater has inlet/outlet isolation valves and a full capacity bypass, drains cascade to the next lower-pressure heater and finally to the condenser, pneumatic level control valves hold normal drain levels, and each heater has a high level dump line to the condenser, controlled by pneumatic valves, for turbine water induction protection.

Case B11B returns all process extraction steam condensate (from CO2 capture and drying) to the deaerator, but SC Case B12B must return it downstream of the condenser, ahead of the condensate polisher, because SC units have no blowdown stream and returning it to the deaerator would let contaminants accumulate. As a result two LP FW heaters are unnecessary in B12B, since the returned condensate lifts FW temperature above what the second LP heater would deliver.

Feedwater (3.1.11.2): one 100 percent turbine-driven BFW pump moves FW out of the deaerator storage tank and through the HP FW heaters into the economizer, with one 25 percent motor-driven BFW pump for startup. Pumps have inlet/outlet isolation valves and individual minimum flow recirculation lines to the deaerator tank, controlled by automatic recirculation valves (combined main-line and bypass check valve, bypass control valve and flow element); startup strainers in the boiler feed pump suction are used at first startup and after major outages or maintenance. HP heaters each have isolation valves and a full capacity bypass, with drains cascading down to the deaerator, pneumatic drain level control, and high level dump lines to the condenser for water induction protection. The deaerator is a horizontal spray tray unit with a storage tank and an internal vent condenser of the direct contact type made of stainless steel (SS). The boiler feed pump turbine runs on main steam up to 60 percent plant load and on IP turbine exhaust extraction above 60 percent.

Main and reheat steam (3.1.11.3): main steam goes from the superheater outlet to the HP turbine stop valves, and reheat steam travels from the HP exhaust into the reheater and onward from its outlet to the stop valves of the IP turbine. Main steam leaves through a motor-operated stop/check valve and motor-operated gate valve in a single line to the HP turbine; a branch off the IP turbine exhaust supplies the boiler feed water pump turbine from about 60 percent load. Cold reheat leaves the HP turbine and passes a flow control valve and a motor-operated isolation gate valve before entering the reheater, and hot reheat leaves via a motor-operated gate valve to the IP turbine. Extraction steam (3.1.11.4) is routed from the HP turbine to heater 7 (and 8 in SC cases), from the IP turbine to heater 6 and the deaerator (heater 5), and from the LP turbine to heaters 1, 2, 3 and 4. Positive closing, balanced disc non-return valves in all extraction lines except those to the condenser-neck LP heaters, placed in horizontal runs as near the turbine as possible, prevent overspeed on trip from flash steam flowing back from the heaters; a turbine trip closes them via relay dumps, and remote manual control of each heater level system returns them to normal check valve duty for restart.

Circulating water (3.1.11.5): the plant is assumed to be supplied by a public water facility and groundwater needing little pretreatment for cooling makeup, with all circulating water filtration and treatment on site. The heat sink is a counter-flow cooling tower of wood frame, mechanical draft construction, served by two 50 percent CWPs; the circulating water system (CWS) cools the condenser, the auxiliary cooling water system and, in capture cases, the CDR facility and CO2 compressors. The auxiliary cooling water system is a CL loop using plate and frame exchangers cooled by circulating water, serving lube oil coolers, the turbine generator, boiler feed pumps and so on, complete with pumps, vacuum breakers, air release valves, instruments and controls. In Cases B11B and B12B the CDR and CO2 compression need a great deal of cooling water from the plant CWS, which is why their CWPs and cooling towers are much larger.

Ash handling (3.1.11.6) conveys, prepares, stores and disposes of each day's fly ash and bottom ash, together with the sorbent and carbon added for mercury control; its scope runs from the bottom ash hoppers, the baghouse hoppers and the collectors under the air heater and economizer to the hydrobins (bottom ash) and the truck filling stations (fly ash); it is sized for 16 hours at 5 percent OP/VWO and 90 days or more at the 100 percent guarantee point. Fly ash from the baghouse and air heaters is pneumatically conveyed with LP blower air to a storage silo and discharged through a wet unloader and telescopic chute into trucks. As noted in Section 3.1.5, ACI and DSI add calcium and filter load, raising particulate by about 26 percent without significantly increasing trace metal leaching. Bottom ash passes a clinker grinder that breaks up clinkers and is sluiced to hydrobins for dewatering and truck removal, and economizer hopper ash and pulverizer pyrites rejects are water-conveyed to an economizer/pyrites transfer tank and periodically sluiced to the hydrobins.

Ducting and stack (3.1.11.7): a single reinforced concrete stack 152 m (500 ft) tall with one fiberglass-reinforced plastic (FRP) liner gives adequate particulate dispersion. Waste treatment/miscellaneous (3.1.11.8): an onsite plant treats runoff, cleaning wastes, blowdown and backwash so the effluent can go to existing systems within EPA limits on suspended solids, oil and grease, pH and miscellaneous metals; it is minimal, mainly neutralization and oil/water separators with pumps and piping. Miscellaneous systems are fuel oil, service air, instrument air and service water, with a tank of No. 2 fuel oil, delivered by truck, for startup and a small auxiliary boiler, and all in-fence truck roads and unloading stations. Buildings and structures (3.1.11.9): foundations support structures, pumps, tanks and other components, and the buildings are the steam turbine building, boiler building, administration and service building, makeup water and pretreatment building, fuel oil pump house, coal crusher building, continuous emissions monitoring building, pump house and electrical equipment building, guard house, runoff water pump house, industrial waste treatment building and FGD system buildings.

The accessory electric plant comprises generator equipment, station service equipment, switchgear and control equipment, wire and cable, and conduit and cable trays, along with the main power transformer, its foundations and standby equipment. Instrumentation and control (3.1.13): a redundant, microprocessor-based, functionally distributed plant-wide DCS monitors and controls all major equipment through multiple video monitor and keyboard units in the control room, which are the main operator interface. It is designed for 99.5 percent availability, and plant and DCS respond automatically to load changes from minimum to 100 percent load; startup and shutdown are supervised manual, with operator-selectable modular automation routines.

Section 3.1.14 defines metrics used in the PC performance summaries. SGE = BH / CH (steam generator efficiency = boiler thermal output divided by coal thermal input), where BH, the heat transferred in the boiler, comes from the Aspen models and CH is coal feed rate times coal heating value. STE = STP / (TI − TC) (steam turbine efficiency = steam turbine power divided by thermal input minus thermal consumption), where TI is taken as the main steam and TC, present only in capture cases, is the enthalpy of steam extracted to serve the capture and CO2 dryer systems minus that of its condensate sent back to the condenser (steam extraction − condensate return). STHR = (1 / STE) * 3,412 (steam turbine heat rate in Btu/kWh = reciprocal of steam turbine efficiency, as a fraction, times 3,412).

Section 3.2 evaluates Cases B11A and B11B, subcritical PC plants of nominal 550 MWe net using a single reheat 16.5 MPa/566°C/566°C (2,400 psig/1,050°F/1,050°F) cycle; the essential difference is that B11B captures CO2 and B11A does not. The section gives, for B11A, a process and system description (only features not already covered in Section 3.1), key assumptions for both cases, the sparing philosophy for both, performance results (performance summary, water balance, carbon/sulfur balances, environmental performance, energy balance table and mass and energy balance diagrams), an equipment list with account codes matching the cost accounts, and cost estimates, followed by the same items for Case B11B.

The subcritical non-capture process follows the block flow diagram (BFD) in Exhibit 3-5, with stream data in Exhibit 3-6. Coal (stream 8) and PA (stream 4) enter through wall-fired burners, and further combustion air including OFA comes from the FD fans (stream 1). The boiler runs slightly below atmospheric pressure so air leaks inward, with infiltration air in stream 7, while streams 3 and 6 are Ljungstrom air preheater leakage from the FD and PA fan outlets into the boiler exhaust. Flue gas passes the SCR reactor, where injected ammonia cuts NOx, then receives hydrated lime (stream 10) for SO3 reduction and passes the combustion air preheater (where the leakages join), leaving at 143°C (289°F) (stream 11); PAC is then injected (stream 12) for mercury, and a fabric filter removes particulate (stream 15). The ID fan raises the gas to 153°C (308°F) and drives it (stream 16) through the FGD, which takes in limestone slurry (stream 17), makeup water (stream 18) and oxidation air (stream 19) and yields product gypsum (stream 20); the clean, saturated gas (stream 21) goes up the stack.

In Case B11A a wet limestone forced oxidation scrubber removes 98 percent of the SO2; its calcium sulfate byproduct is dewatered and stored on site, and although the wallboard grade material might be sold, no credit is taken because that depends heavily on local markets. Saturated scrubber exit gas goes up the stack. LNBs and OFA hold NOx to about 0.5 lb/MMBtu and the SCR cuts it a further 83 percent to 0.08 lb/MMBtu. A pulse jet fabric filter removes particulate at 99.9 percent efficiency. Together SCR, ACI, fabric filter, DSI and wet FGD lower mercury emissions by 96.8 percent. CO2 leaves uncontrolled. For the carbon balance, carbon enters with the coal, the air, PAC and the FGD limestone reagent (air carbon is kept because the Aspen model tracks air components throughout) and leaves mainly as stack CO2, with the PAC caught in the fabric filter and some carbon in the gypsum.

paragraphs.section: 3.2.7 Case B11B – PC Subcritical Unit with CO2 Capture
paragraphs.text: Case B11B is the B11A subcritical PC plant with a Cansolv CDR facility added. Net output is held at a nominal 550 MW by enlarging the boiler and turbine/generator to cover the extra auxiliary load imposed by CO2 compressors and the CDR facility; in contrast to the NGCC cases, whose gross output is set by available CT sizes, PC boilers and steam turbines can be bought at almost any output, so constant net output is achievable. Apart from the added CO2 capture and compression the process matches B11A; its BFD and stream tables are Exhibit 3-22 and Exhibit 3-23, and the CDR process is not re-described since Section 3.1.8 covers it.

Case B11B uses the modeling assumptions of Section 3.2.2 and produces 550 MW net at a net plant efficiency of 31.2 percent (HHV basis); Exhibit 3-24 summarizes performance and Exhibit 3-25 breaks down auxiliary power. The CDR facility with CO2 compression takes more than half of the auxiliary load, and the CWS (CWPs and cooling tower fan) more than 13 percent, mostly because the CDR facility and CO2 compressors need so much cooling water.

In Case B11B the wet limestone forced oxidation scrubber again removes 98 percent of SO2, with its wallboard grade calcium sulfate dewatered and stored on site and no byproduct credit taken given local market dependence. A NaOH based polishing scrubber in the CDR facility then lowers SO2 to 1 ppmv, and the CDR absorber removes essentially all of the rest, so SO2 emissions are very low. LNBs and OFA hold NOx to about 0.5 lb/MMBtu and the SCR removes a further 85 percent, to 0.07 lb/MMBtu; the pulse jet fabric filter works at 99.9 percent; and the combined SCR, ACI, fabric filter, DSI and wet FGD reduce mercury emissions by 97.2 percent. The CDR facility removes ninety percent of flue gas CO2. Carbon enters with coal, air, PAC and FGD limestone and leaves mostly as stack CO2, plus PAC in the fabric filter and some in gypsum.

Carbon capture efficiency = (1 − (Carbon in Stack / Total Carbon In)) * 100 = (1 − 33,446 / 335,258) * 100 = 90.0% (one minus the fraction of total carbon input that leaves in the stack gas, in lb/hr).
