Section 3.3 evaluates Cases B12A and B12B, both supercritical (SC) PC plants sized for a nominal 550 MWe net output and both operating a 24.1 MPa/593°C/593°C (3,500 psig/1,100°F/1,100°F) steam cycle with single reheat; B12B adds CO2 capture and is otherwise identical to B12A. The material follows the same layout as the subcritical PC section: the process and system description for B12A, the key assumptions and the sparing philosophy shared by B12A and B12B, then B12A performance results, equipment list and cost estimates, and finally the description, performance, equipment list and costs for B12B.

This subsection covers the SC PC process without CO2 capture. Because it is almost the same as the non-capture subcritical PC description, it is restated only so the section is complete. Stream numbers refer to the block flow diagram (BFD) of Exhibit 3-37, and Exhibit 3-38 tabulates process data for those numbered streams. Coal (stream 8) and primary air, PA (stream 4), enter the boiler through wall-fired burners, while the FD fans supply the remaining combustion air, OFA included (stream 1). Since the furnace is held slightly below atmospheric pressure, air leaks inward; this infiltration air is stream 7. Leakage across the Ljungstrom air preheater from the FD and PA fan discharges into the boiler exhaust is represented by streams 3 and 6.

Leaving the boiler, the flue gas goes through the SCR reactor, where hydrated lime is added (stream 10) to cut SO3. It then crosses the combustion air preheater, picking up the preheater leakage, where its temperature falls to 143°C (289°F) (stream 11); next PAC is injected (stream 12) to reduce mercury. A fabric filter removes particulate (stream 15). The ID fan, which raises the gas temperature to 153°C (308°F), drives the flue gas (stream 16) through the FGD unit, which takes in limestone slurry (stream 17), makeup water (stream 18) and oxidation air (stream 19) and discharges gypsum product (stream 20). The cleaned, water-saturated gas leaving the FGD (stream 21) flows to the stack and is released to atmosphere.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.2.1 Balance of Plant – Cases B12A and B12B
paragraphs.text: The balance of plant assumptions for B12A and B12B are the same as for every other case and were already listed in Exhibit 3-8.

The design uses single trains wherever possible, adding a second train only when equipment capacity demands it, and provides no redundancy apart from the usual spares for rotating equipment. Main subsystems and their sparing: PC SC boiler, wall-fired and dry-bottom, 1 x 100%; SCR reactors, 2 x 50%; DSI system, 1 x 100%; ACI system, 1 x 100%; fabric filters (single-stage, in-line, multi-compartment), 2 x 50%; absorber of the wet limestone forced oxidation type operating at positive pressure, 1 x 100%; steam turbine, 1 x 100%; and, only for Case B12B, a CO2 absorption system (absorber, stripper and ancillary equipment) at 1 x 100% plus CO2 compression systems at 2 x 50%.

SO2 is removed at 98 percent efficiency in a wet limestone forced oxidation scrubber. Its calcium sulfate byproduct is dewatered and kept on site; although this wallboard grade gypsum could in principle be sold, no byproduct credit is assumed because any sale would hinge on local markets. The water-saturated gas from the scrubber leaves through the stack. LNBs and OFA hold NOx to roughly 0.5 lb/MMBtu, and the SCR then lowers it by a further 83 percent to 0.09 lb/MMBtu. A pulse jet fabric filter captures particulate at 99.9 percent efficiency. Taken together, the SCR, ACI, fabric filter, DSI and wet FGD cut mercury emissions by 96.7 percent. CO2 leaves the process without any control.

Exhibit 3-45 gives the plant's overall water balance. Water demand is the total water a given process needs; part of it is met by water recovered inside the plant and reused as internal recycle, and demand minus recycle equals raw water withdrawal. Raw water withdrawal means water taken from the ground or diverted from a POTW for plant use, assumed here to come half from a POTW and half from groundwater; it can be viewed as the metered raw water used for every plant purpose, for example cooling tower, FGD and BFW makeup. Withdrawal minus process water discharge is water consumption, i.e. the share of withdrawn water that is evaporated, transpired, built into products or otherwise not returned to its source, and it expresses the plant's net effect on the water source balance.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.7 Case B12B – Supercritical PC with CO2 Capture
paragraphs.text: Case B12B keeps the B12A SC PC configuration but adds a CDR facility based on the Cansolv system. Net output stays at the nominal 550 MW because the boiler and the turbine/generator are enlarged to cover the extra auxiliary load of the CDR facility and the CO2 compressors. This is possible for PC plants, unlike the NGCC cases whose gross output is set by the sizes in which CTs are available, since boilers and steam turbines can be bought at almost any required output, allowing a constant net output. Apart from the CO2 capture addition, the B12B process description is effectively that of B12A; Exhibit 3-53 gives the BFD and Exhibit 3-54 the stream tables, and the CDR facility itself is not described again because Section 3.1.8 already covers it.

B12B uses the modeling assumptions already given in Section 3.3.2. It delivers 550 MW net with a 32.5 percent net plant efficiency on an HHV basis. Exhibit 3-55 summarizes overall performance and Exhibit 3-56 itemizes auxiliary power. More than half of the auxiliary load is attributable to the CDR facility together with CO2 compression, and the CWS (CWPs plus cooling tower fans) takes close to 13 percent, mostly because the CDR facility and CO2 compressors need a large amount of cooling water.

As in B12A, a wet limestone forced oxidation scrubber removes 98 percent of the SO2, and the dewatered calcium sulfate is stored on site with no byproduct credit, since a market for the wallboard grade material depends on local conditions. A NaOH based polishing scrubber in the CDR facility then brings SO2 down to 1 ppmv, and the CDR absorber vessel takes out practically all of what is left, so SO2 emissions are very low. LNBs and OFA limit NOx to about 0.5 lb/MMBtu, after which the SCR cuts it by 85 percent to 0.08 lb/MMBtu. The pulse jet fabric filter removes particulate at 99.9 percent efficiency, the combined SCR, ACI, fabric filter, DSI and wet FGD lower mercury emissions by 97.1 percent, and the CDR facility strips out ninety (90) percent of flue-gas CO2.

Carbon enters the plant with the coal, the air, the PAC and the FGD limestone reagent, and it leaves mostly as stack CO2, with the PAC retained in the fabric filter and part of the carbon exiting with the gypsum. Carbon capture efficiency is defined as one minus the ratio of stack-gas carbon to total carbon input, evaluated as: Carbon in Stack / (Total Carbon In) = (1 − (32,112 / 321,883)) * 100 = 90.0% (capture efficiency in percent = (1 − stack carbon / total carbon in, both in lb/hr) × 100; the left-hand label is printed as shown in the source).

Power out is the steam turbine output before generator losses, and the generator terminal power reported in Exhibit 3-55 is power out multiplied by a 98.5 percent generator efficiency. The capture process heat out stream is heat sent to cooling water and finally to ambient through the cooling tower, as is the condenser heat out stream; the CO2 compressor intercooler duty is counted within the capture process heat out stream.

Performance observations. Adding CO2 capture and compression lowers efficiency by 7.8 absolute percentage points in the subcritical PC case and by 8.2 in the SC PC case. The drop comes from the heavy auxiliary demand of the capture process and CO2 compression and from the much larger cooling water need, which raises CWP and cooling tower fan loads; auxiliary load grows by 63 MW (subcritical) and 62 MW (SC). Because the PC cases include wet FGD, SO2 emissions can stand in for HCl (ref. 17): under the MATS regulation, meeting the SO2 limit allows the HCl limit to be treated as met. Without capture, SO2 emissions of the two technologies are almost the same, though the subcritical case is higher per unit of gross output owing to its lower efficiency; in the capture cases the polishing scrubber and absorber vessel make SO2 emissions negligible. Uncontrolled CO2 emissions per unit mass are likewise higher for subcritical than for SC because of lower efficiency, and capture reduces carbon by 90 percent in both. Exhibit 3-69 shows the TOC components and overall TASC for each PC case.

Figure captions for the PC case summary (paraphrased; source for all: NETL): Exhibit 3-69 charts plant capital cost of the PC cases; Exhibit 3-70 charts PC-case COE, with a footnote saying the non-capture cases are financed conventionally while all others use high-risk financial assumptions consistent with the NETL QGESS on cost estimation methodology for power plant performance assessments (ref. 1); Exhibit 3-71 plots how PC-case COE responds to capacity factor; Exhibit 3-72 plots how PC-case COE responds to coal price; Exhibit 3-73 charts the CO2 captured and CO2 avoided costs of the PC cases; Exhibit 3-74 charts PC-case raw water withdrawal and consumption.

Observations on TOC (Exhibit 3-69): without capture, the SC PC TOC exceeds the subcritical PC TOC by about 3.2 percent, and with capture the SC plant is about 1.6 percent above the subcritical one. Adding CO2 capture raises TOC by 76 percent in the subcritical case and 73 percent in the SC case. Besides the expensive capture process itself, the capture cases need considerably costlier cooling towers and CWPs because of their greater cooling water demand, and gross output must rise by 63 MW (subcritical) and 62 MW (SC) to keep net output at 550 MW; the larger gross output means more coal flow and therefore higher costs in every cost account. Exhibit 3-70 presents COE for the four PC cases, including T&S for the capture cases.

COE observations. Capital is the biggest COE component in every case, most markedly with CO2 capture, and fuel is second; capital charges plus fuel make up 72 to 77 percent of the total throughout. Without capture, the SC case's slightly higher capital cost is nearly cancelled by its better efficiency, so its COE is only about 0.3 percent above subcritical even though its TOC is over 3 percent higher. With capture, the capital increase is smaller still and the efficiency benefit more than compensates, leaving SC PC COE roughly 0.2 percent below subcritical despite a TOC close to 2 percent higher. In both pairs (non-capture subcritical vs SC, and the two capture cases) the COE difference is well inside the study's accuracy limits.

Exhibit 3-71 shows how COE varies with capacity factor; the curves assume that capacity factors above 85 percent are reachable without spending additional capital. The subcritical and SC curves almost coincide, so the two lines are hard to tell apart, and COE climbs a little faster at low CF because the comparatively large capital component is divided among fewer kilowatt-hours. Exhibit 3-72 shows that PC COE depends only weakly on fuel price: tripling the coal price from $1 to $3/MMBtu raises COE by roughly 26 percent without capture and 18 percent with CO2 capture.

Using the method of Section 2.7.4, the costs of CO2 captured and CO2 avoided were computed for the PC capture cases with SC PC taken as the non-capture reference; Exhibit 3-73 shows that the subcritical and SC results are almost the same. Exhibit 3-74 then gives, for each PC case, normalized values of raw water withdrawal, process discharge and consumption.

Cooling tower makeup dominates raw water consumption in all PC cases, representing about 81 percent of raw water without capture and 85 percent with capture. Capture cases consume much more raw water because the capture process needs cooling water to: lower the flue gas from 56°C (133°F) at the FGD exit to the 30°C (86°F) operating temperature of the CO2 absorber, which also condenses water out of the FGD-saturated gas; reject the heat brought in by stripping steam so the solvent is cooled; remove the heat from auxiliary electric loads; and remove heat in the CO2 compressor intercoolers. Cooling the flue gas to absorber temperature also recovers extra water in the capture cases, and this condensate is treated and reused as cooling tower makeup.

Section 4 presents two natural gas combined cycle (NGCC) configurations. Both rely on market-ready technology assumed to be commercially available in time for plant start-up, and both use a multi-shaft 2x2x1 arrangement in which a pair of state-of-the-art 2013 F-class CTGs feeds a pair of HRSGs serving a single STG. The cases are compared with and without CO2 capture on the same thermal input; because the CDR facility and the CO2 compressors add auxiliary load, the capture design delivers less net power. Since gross output is essentially fixed by the output of the commercially available CT, a comparison at equal net output could not be made. The Rankine (bottoming) cycle in both designs is a single reheat steam cycle at 16.5 MPa/566°C/566°C (2,400 psig/1,050°F/1,050°F). More aggressive steam conditions were examined but rejected, because very few operating HRSGs could support them (ref. 28).

Cases B31A and B31B share almost the same configuration; the only difference is that B31B adds CO2 capture and B31A has none. This section describes the process areas common to both plant configurations.

The study assumes that a natural gas main of sufficient capacity runs within 16 km (10 mi) of the site fence line and that a right-of-way is available for a branch line to the plant. Gas is taken to be delivered at 3.0 MPa (435 psig) and 38°C (100ºF) at the custody transfer point of the plant, which satisfies the fuel system requirements of the state-of-the-art 2013 F-class turbine; therefore no pressure reducing station with gas preheating (normally used to avoid moisture and hydrocarbon condensation) and no fuel booster compressor are needed. In line with Section 2.4.2, a mercaptan addition of 5.75x10^-6 mol% is assumed in the gas (ref. 11). A new on-site gas metering station is assumed next to the new CT; the meter can be either a rate-of-flow type feeding the plant computer for totalizing and recording, or a positive displacement type, and either way a full time-based record of consumption rate and cumulative consumption is kept.

Two CTGs form the basis of the combined cycle plant. Each represents a state-of-the-art 2013 F-class turbine with an ISO base rating of 211 MW on natural gas (ref. 18); it is a constant speed, single spool, axial flow machine fitted with variable IGVs and a dry LNB combustion system. Every CTG comes with inlet air filtration and inlet silencers, lube and control oil systems with cooling, electric motor starting, acoustical enclosures with heating and ventilation, control systems (including supervisory control), fire protection and fuel systems. No backup fuel is provided in these cases. The CTG is normally delivered as several shop-fabricated modules that already contain the mechanical, electrical and control systems needed for operation, so site work consists of interconnecting the modules and tying them to plant systems. Although project specific, the CTG scope of supply for combined cycle service changes little between projects; a typical scope is listed in Exhibit 4-1.

Starting system: scope=enclosure, starting motor or static start system, turning gear and clutch assembly, starting clutch, torque converter. Generator: scope=static or rotating exciter (with an excitation transformer for a static system), line termination enclosure with CTs, VTs, surge arrestors and surge capacitors, neutral cubicle with CT, neutral tie bus, grounding transformer and secondary resistor, generator gas dryer, seal oil system (defoaming tank, reservoir, seal oil pump, emergency seal oil pump, vapor extractor, oil mist eliminator), generator auxiliaries control enclosure, generator breaker, iso-phase bus between generator and breaker, grounding system connectors. Generator cooling: scope=Totally Enclosed Water-to-Air-Cooled (TEWAC) system (circulation system, interconnecting piping and controls) or hydrogen cooling system (H2 to glycol and glycol to air heat exchangers, liquid level detector circulation system, interconnecting piping and controls). Miscellaneous: scope=interconnecting pipe, wire, tubing and cable; instrument air system including air dryer; on line and off line water wash system; LP CO2 storage tank; drain system; drain tanks; coupling, coupling cover and associated hardware.

The CT package also includes the electrical generators. These are assumed to be 3-phase, 60 Hz, 24 kV machines built to American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) standards for turbine-driven synchronous generators. The generator is of the TEWAC type and comes complete with its excitation system, cooling and protective relaying.

The HRSG has three steam drums (HP, IP and LP) together with superheater, reheater and economizer sections. The HP boiler feed pump supplies FW to the HP drum, where HP steam is raised and then sent to the superheater section and heated to 566°C (1,050°F). The IP boiler feed pump supplies FW to the IP drum; IP drum steam is superheated to 482°C (900°F), mixed with the exhaust of the HP turbine, and the mixture is reheated to 566°C (1,050ºF) before entering the IP section of the steam turbine. Steam from the LP drum feeds the LP turbine.

Condensate and FW are heated in the economizer sections, each in its own tube bundle. HRSG tubes are generally bare and/or finned tubing or pipe. Type P91 or P22 ferritic alloy is used in the high-temperature parts, while carbon steel (CS) is used where temperatures stay below 399°C [750°F]. Each HRSG discharges straight to its stack, which is built of CS plate with a Type 409 SS lining; for the NGCC cases the stack is taken as 46 m (150 ft) tall, and its cost is carried in the HRSG account.

NOx is reduced by two measures. The first is the DLN burner of the CTG, a low NOx design that brings emissions down to about 9 ppmvd (ref. 18), taken as roughly 98 percent NO and referenced to 15 percent O2. Although a state-of-the-art 2013 F-class CT by itself already emits NOx below the limits given in Section 2.4.2, an SCR was added as the second measure so that the plant installs BACT and satisfies the EPA PSD program. The SCR reduces NO to N2 and H2O with ammonia over a catalyst; it comprises a reactor plus an ammonia supply and storage system, and is designed for 90 percent reduction when firing natural gas (ref. 19).

Operation description: inside the HRSG, the SCR reactor is placed in the gas stream between the HP and IP sections. It holds one catalyst layer made of modules stacked in line on a structural support frame, and space is left for adding a further layer. Ammonia is injected into the gas just upstream of the reactor through an injection grid divided into several sections, each made of multiple pipes with nozzles; the ammonia flow to each section is controlled to account for uneven flue gas flow distribution across the HRSG. The catalyst promotes the reaction of ammonia with NOx and is made of active materials such as titanium dioxide, vanadium pentoxide and tungsten trioxide; its optimum inlet flue gas temperature range is 260°C (500°F) to 343°C (650°F). The ammonia storage and injection system comprises unloading facilities, a bulk storage tank, vaporizers and a dilution air skid.
terms: between the HP and IP sections

paragraphs.text: In Case B31B a CDR facility removes 90 percent of the CO2 from the flue gas leaving the HRSG, purifies it and compresses it to a SC condition; all carbon in the natural gas is assumed to end up as CO2. The CDR consists of flue gas supply, CO2 absorption, solvent stripping and reclaiming, and CO2 compression and drying. Absorption, stripping and solvent reclaiming in Case B31B follow the Cansolv system described in Section 3.1.8, except that no SO2 polishing step is needed: pipeline gas sulfur yields flue gas SO2 already below the outlet concentration of the polishing scrubber used in the PC cases. The gas case gains little from its much lower chloride input (chloride forms HSS in the absorber) and lower flue gas SO2 and NOx (which contribute to amine degradation), because the prescrubber in the coal cases already removes most of these contaminants.

Compared with the PC cases, the NGCC flue gas has a larger volumetric flow (147 million ft3/hr in Case B31B versus 90 million ft3/hr in Case B12B) and a lower CO2 concentration (4.9 mol% in B31B versus 12.9 mol% in B12B). As a result the gas case needs a CO2 absorber more than 1.5 times the size of the coal case absorber, while its lower CO2 content means the B31B CO2 stripper is only 40 percent of the volume of the B12B stripper.

The turbine combines HP and IP sections with a double-flow LP section, all sharing one shaft with the generator; HP and IP share a single-span, opposed-flow casing and the LP section has its own casing. Main steam from the boiler passes the stop and control valves and enters at 16.5 MPa/566°C (2,400 psig/1,050°F) near the middle of the HP span. After expanding through the HP section it is joined by steam from the IP superheater and sent back to the HRSG for reheating. Reheat steam returns through reheat stop and intercept valves into the IP section at 4.2 MPa/566°C (608 psia/1,050°F). IP exhaust goes through a cross-over pipe to the LP section; a branch line with combined stop/intercept valves brings LP steam from the HRSG LP drum into the cross-over. The flow splits into two paths through the LP sections, which exhaust downward to the condenser.

A CL pressurized oil system with water cooling supplies bearing lubrication. Shaft sealing against air in-leakage and steam blowout uses a modern positive pressure, variable clearance arrangement tied to a LP steam seal system. Power is generated at 24 kV by an open-air-cooled generator with a static, transformer type exciter. STG control is by a triple-redundant, microprocessor-based electro-hydraulic system that gives digital control according to programmed algorithms, color monitor/operator interfaces, datalinks to the balance-of-plant DCS, and on-line repair capability.

The condensate system moves condensate from the condenser hotwell to the deaerator passing on the way through the gland steam condenser and the HRSG low-temperature economizer section. It includes one main condenser, two motor-driven vertical multistage condensate pumps of 50 percent capacity each (two for the whole plant), a gland steam condenser, vacuum pumps for condenser air removal, a condensate polisher, and an HRSG low-temperature tube bundle. The pumps discharge through separate lines, each with a check valve and gate valve, into a common header, and a shared minimum-flow recirculation line back to the condenser keeps the required minimum flow through the gland steam condenser and the condensate pumps.

The feedwater (FW) system delivers the various FW streams from the HRSG deaerator storage tank to their respective steam drums. Each HRSG has one 100 percent capacity motor-driven feed pump (two pumps for the plant), and the pumps have an interstage takeoff supplying IP and LP FW. Every pump has inlet and outlet isolation valves, outlet check valves and its own minimum-flow recirculation line back to the deaerator storage tank, with recirculation governed by pneumatic flow control valves. Startup strainers on the boiler feed pump suctions are used during first startup and after major outages or maintenance.

Main, intermediate and low pressure steam leave the superheater section of the HRSG via motor-operated stop/check valves followed by motor-operated gate valves. Main steam goes to the HP turbine stop valve. Intermediate steam is merged with the HP turbine exhaust and routed via a motor-operated isolation gate valve into the HRSG reheater, after which reheated steam passes a further motor-operated gate valve on its way to the IP turbines. Low pressure steam joins the IP turbine exhaust and passes through a motor-operated isolation gate valve to the LP turbines.

The CWS supplies cooling water to condense the main turbine exhaust, to serve the auxiliary cooling system and, in Case B31B, for the CDR facility. It consists of two 50 percent capacity vertical CWPs (two for the plant), an evaporative cooling tower of mechanical draft type and the connecting piping. The condenser is a single pass horizontal unit with divided water boxes, each containing two separate circulating water circuits, so that half of the condenser can be taken out of service for cleaning or tube plugging during normal operation at reduced load.

The auxiliary cooling system is a CL system using plate and frame heat exchangers cooled by circulating water. It serves: (1) CTG lube oil coolers, (2) CTG air coolers, (3) STG lube oil coolers, (4) STG hydrogen coolers, (5) boiler feed water pumps, (6) air compressors, (7) generator seal oil coolers where applicable, (8) sample room chillers, (9) blowdown coolers and (10) condensate extraction pump-motor coolers. In Case B31B the CDR system draws a large cooling water flow from the NGCC plant CWS, which is why the CWPs and cooling tower are considerably larger in that case.

The structures assumed for the NGCC cases are: (1) a generation building that houses the STG, (2) a CWP house, (3) an administration/office/control room/maintenance building, (4) a water treatment building and (5) a fire water pump house.

Included in the accessory electric plant are all switchgear and control equipment, the generator and station service equipment, conduit, cable trays, wire and cable, together with the main transformer, required foundations and standby equipment.

All runoff, cleaning wastes, blowdown and backwash are treated in an onsite facility, and the treated water is expected to be dischargeable to existing systems while meeting EPA limits on suspended solids, oil and grease, pH and miscellaneous metals. Waste treatment is minimal, mainly neutralization and oil/water separators with their pumps and piping. Service air, instrument air and service water systems are provided, as are all truck roadways and unloading stations inside the fence.

A redundant, microprocessor-based, functionally distributed DCS covers the whole plant. The control room contains video monitors and keyboard units that serve as the main interface between operators and the process. The DCS handles monitoring and control of all major equipment and is designed for 99.5 percent availability. Plant equipment and the DCS respond automatically to load changes between minimum load and 100 percent, while startup and shutdown are run as supervised manual procedures in which the operator can select modular automation routines.

This section explains how several metrics in the NGCC performance summaries are computed. Combustion turbine efficiency: CTE = CTP / TI (combustion turbine efficiency = CT power produced ÷ thermal input to the turbines), where CTE is combustion turbine efficiency, CTP is combustion turbine power and TI is thermal input to the turbines. The thermal input is obtained by multiplying the natural gas feed rate by the gas heating value and converting the result to kW.

Steam turbine efficiency: STE = STP / (TI − TC) (steam turbine efficiency = steam turbine power ÷ (thermal input − thermal consumption)), where STE is steam turbine efficiency, STP is steam turbine power, TI is thermal input and TC is thermal consumption. Here the thermal input equals the enthalpy of the flue gas entering the HRSG minus the enthalpy of the flue gas leaving the HRSG. Thermal consumption exists only in the capture cases and is the enthalpy difference between steam drawn off to serve the capture and CO2 dryer systems and the condensate returning to the condenser (steam extraction – condensate return).

Steam turbine heat rate is the reciprocal of steam turbine efficiency expressed in heat-rate units: STHR = (1 / STE) ∗ 3,412 (steam turbine heat rate in Btu/kWh = 3,412 ÷ steam turbine efficiency as a fraction), where STHR is steam turbine heat rate, Btu/kWh, and STE is steam turbine efficiency, fraction.

Exhibit 4-11 gives the Case B31A water balance. Water demand is the total water a process needs; part of it is recovered in the process and reused as internal recycle, and demand minus recycle is the raw water withdrawal. Raw water withdrawal means water taken from the ground or diverted from surface water for plant use, here assumed to come 50 percent from a POTW and 50 percent from groundwater; it corresponds to water metered from a raw water source and used for any plant purpose, such as condenser and cooling tower makeup. Water consumption is withdrawal minus process water discharge, i.e., the share of withdrawn raw water that is evaporated, transpired, built into products or otherwise not returned to its source, and so it expresses the plant's net effect on the water source balance.

paragraphs.section: 4.2.7 Case B31B – NGCC with CO2 Capture
paragraphs.text: Case B31B uses the same plant layout as Case B31A except that CDR technology is added to capture CO2. Nominal net output falls to 559 MW, because the CT design output cannot change while the CDR facility adds a large auxiliary power load; in addition, the steam drawn by the CDR facility lowers the steam turbine output. Apart from the added CO2 capture, the B31B process description is essentially that of B31A; its BFD is Exhibit 4-18 and its stream tables are in Exhibit 4-19. The CDR facility process was already described in Section 4.1.5 and is not repeated.

The modeling assumptions for Case B31B were given in Section 4.2.2. The plant's net output is 559 MW and its net plant efficiency 45.7 percent (HHV basis); Exhibit 4-20 summarizes overall performance and Exhibit 4-21 itemizes the auxiliary power. More than 67 percent of the auxiliary load comes from the CDR facility including CO2 compression, and close to 16 percent from the CWS (CWPs and cooling tower fan), mostly because the CDR facility demands so much cooling water.

As in Case B31A, gas sulfur is taken as an average 0.34 gr/100 scf (4.71x10^-4 lb-S/MMBtu) (ref. 11), all of it from the added mercaptan (CH4S), so no sulfur capture equipment is required. NOx is held to about 1.0 ppmvd (at 15 percent O2) by the CTG DLN burner (about 9 ppmvd at 15 percent O2, ref. 18) followed by an SCR designed for 90 percent NO reduction (ref. 19). With no PM, Hg or HCl assumed in pipeline gas, these emissions are zero. Relative to coal at equal output, CO2 is lower owing to the higher heat content and lower carbon intensity of gas and the higher efficiency of NGCC. In addition, the CDR facility removes 90 percent of the flue gas CO2.

Carbon enters Case B31B in the natural gas and in the CT air, and leaves as CO2 in the stack gas, in the CO2 dryer vent and in the captured CO2 product (Exhibit 4-23). Carbon capture efficiency is one minus the ratio of stack-gas carbon to total carbon in, times 100: (1 − (Carbon in Stack / Total Carbon In)) ∗ 100 = (1 − 13,506 / 135,061) ∗ 100 = 90.0% (capture efficiency = share of incoming carbon that does not leave through the stack, using lb/hr values).

Observations on plant performance from Exhibit 4-32: the NGCC without CO2 capture reaches 51.5 percent efficiency on an HHV basis. Gas Turbine World gives an estimated 58.0 percent (LHV basis) for a gas-fired state-of-the-art 2013 F-class turbine in combined cycle service (ref. 44); converted to LHV, this report's value is 57.0 percent. Adding CO2 capture costs 5.8 absolute percentage points of efficiency, mainly because of the capture system and CO2 compression auxiliary loads and the much larger cooling water need, which raises the CWP and cooling tower fan loads; overall, capture adds 31 MW of auxiliary load relative to the non-capture case.

Exhibit 4-33 shows the TOC components and overall TASC of the two NGCC cases. CO2 capture more than doubles the NGCC TOC; the process contingency for the capture process is $75/kW, roughly 4 percent of TOC. Exhibit 4-33 Plant capital cost for NGCC cases (source: NETL). Exhibit 4-34 indicates that, at the study gas price, fuel is a large share of COE: 71 percent of the total without capture and 53 percent with capture, while CO2 T&S accounts for only 5 percent of COE in the capture case. Exhibit 4-34 COE of NGCC cases (source: NETL).

Exhibit 4-35 shows how NGCC COE varies with CF. Because the capital component is relatively small, NGCC COE is fairly insensitive to CF but strongly sensitive to fuel cost (Exhibit 4-36): when CF falls, the drop in net generation is almost balanced by a matching drop in fuel cost. Raising the natural gas price by 33 percent, from $6.13 to $8.15/MMBtu, lifts COE by 23 percent without capture and by 17 percent with capture; the higher capital cost of the capture case slightly damps the effect of fuel price changes. Exhibit 4-35 Sensitivity of COE to capacity factor in NGCC cases (source: NETL). Exhibit 4-36 Sensitivity of COE to fuel price in NGCC cases (source: NETL).

First-year costs of CO2 avoided and captured were computed with the method and equations of Section 2.7.4 and are shown for the NGCC cases in Exhibit 4-37. Taking the NGCC without capture as reference, CO2 captured costs $71/tonne ($65/ton) and CO2 avoided costs $94/tonne ($85/ton). Exhibit 4-37 First year cost of CO2 captured and avoided in NGCC cases (source: NETL). Exhibit 4-38 presents normalized water withdrawal, process discharge and raw water consumption. Exhibit 4-38 Raw water withdrawal and consumption in NGCC cases (source: NETL).

Water observations: in the capture case, normalized water withdrawal rises by 71 percent and normalized raw water consumption by 66 percent, because the capture process needs a lot of cooling water and therefore much more cooling tower makeup. Cooling tower makeup makes up about 99 percent of raw water consumption in both NGCC cases. Without capture, BFW blowdown recycled to the cooling tower is the only internal recycle stream; with capture, condensate recovered from the flue gas while it is during its cooling to the 30°C (86°F) absorber temperature is also sent back to the cooling tower.

Exhibit 5-2 plots net plant efficiency on an HHV basis. Main conclusions: the NGCC cases are the most efficient of all technologies, at 51.5 percent without and 45.7 percent with CO2 capture, followed by the non-capture SC PC case at 40.7 percent. Capture lowers PC efficiency by 20 percent in relative terms (8 percentage points) and NGCC efficiency by 11 percent relative (6 percentage points). The NGCC penalty is smaller because natural gas is less carbon intensive than coal (with the study fuel compositions, 32 lb carbon/MMBtu of heat input for gas versus 56 lb/MMBtu for coal), and because the more efficient non-capture NGCC has less CO2 to capture and compress (its CO2 emissions are about 54-56 percent below the PC cases at equal net output). These advantages are partly offset by the lower CO2 concentration in NGCC flue gas (4% vs. 13% for PC); per lb of CO2 captured, the energy penalty is 0.16 kWh for NGCC and 0.13 kWh for PC. Exhibit 5-2 Net plant efficiency (HHV basis) (source: NETL).

Because natural gas contains no Hg, PM or HCl, its environmental profile compares favorably with the PC cases. The report assumes that the only sulfur in the gas comes from the added odorant, mercaptan, which keeps the SO2 emission rate under the regulatory limits without additional control. For every case, PC and NGCC alike, the estimated Hg, PM, NOx and SO2 emissions are at or below the regulatory limits now in force.

Exhibit 5-3 gives three water values per technology, each normalized by net output: raw water withdrawal, process discharge and raw water consumption. Exhibit 5-3 Raw water withdrawal and consumption (source: NETL). Conclusions: NGCC consumes the least raw water of all cases, with and without capture; the normalized raw water consumption ratio is 2.2:1.0 (SCPC:NGCC), as expected since the PC cases have larger steam turbine output and hence larger condenser duties, cooling water flows and cooling water makeup. CO2 capture adds a substantial water demand for every technology, because post-combustion capture needs much cooling water, raising cooling tower blowdown and evaporative losses; normalized raw water consumption grows by 62 percent for NGCC, 50 percent for SC PC and 48 percent for subcritical PC. These relative increases mirror the smaller non-capture water needs that follow from lower steam turbine output. Even with smaller relative increases, PC still has the largest normalized raw water consumption among capture technologies, at 2.0:1.0 (PC: NGCC).

Exhibit 5-5 shows the normalized TOC components and overall TASC for each technology. Conclusions: on a TOC ($/kW) basis, NGCC capital cost is about 34% of PC capital cost without capture and 42% with capture. Part of this NGCC advantage stems from not needing the emission control equipment that PC requires to meet current regulations. CO2 capture strongly affects every technology, with TOC rising 76 percent (subcritical PC), 73 percent (SC PC) and 115 percent (NGCC). Exhibit 5-5 Plant capital costs (source: NETL); TOC is in 2011 dollars, whereas TASC is in 2011 to 2015 mixed-year dollars for PC and 2011 to 2013 mixed-year dollars for NGCC.

Exhibit 5-6 is introduced in the text as a graph of net plant efficiency (HHV basis), although its caption is COE by cost component. Main conclusions: NGCC COE is 70% of PC COE without capture and 61% with capture. In PC cases the capital cost component is the biggest share of COE (46-51 percent of total COE) while in NGCC cases it is 21-31 percent; fuel is the biggest component for NGCC (53-71 percent) but only 22-31 percent for PC. CO2 T&S adds $4/MWh (NGCC) to $10/MWh (PC), under 7 percent of total COE for every capture case. Although capture raised NGCC TOC the most, the small capital share of non-capture NGCC (where fuel dominates COE) means NGCC COE rose less than PC COE (52 percent versus 74-75 percent). Exhibit 5-6 COE by cost component (source: NETL).

If future legislation puts a price on carbon emissions, every technology studied would become more costly; plants without capture would be hit harder than those with capture, and coal-based plants harder than gas-based ones. In Exhibit 5-7 the cost of CO2 avoided appears where the PC capture case lines cross the SC PC non-capture line, and where the NGCC capture line crosses the NGCC non-capture line; for instance, NGCC at $93.8/tonne ($85.1/ton) and SC PC at $89.4/tonne ($81.1/ton). The curves use the study design capacity factor (85 percent capacity factor) and fuel prices of $2.78/GJ ($2.94/MMBtu) for coal and $5.81/GJ ($6.13 /MMBtu) for natural gas. Exhibit 5-7 Impact of carbon emissions price on study technologies (source: NETL).

From the carbon emissions price graph: the effect of the CO2 emission price on COE cannot be distinguished between subcritical PC and SC PC, for both capture and non-capture cases. Under baseline study conditions, non-capture SC PC moves rapidly away from non-capture NGCC as the CO2 emission cost rises, owing to the lower carbon intensity of gas and the higher NGCC efficiency. Exhibit 5-8 is a "phase diagram" type plot of CO2 emission price against natural gas price, whose lines mark cost parity between pairs of technologies. Exhibit 5-8 Lowest cost power generation options comparing NGCC and PC (source: NETL). It shows that non-capture plants are cheapest below a CO2 price of $78/tonne ($71/ton); NGCC is always preferred below a gas price of $10/MMBtu (at an 85 percent capacity factor); and coal plants are always preferred above $15/MMBtu.

Revenue from selling captured CO2 for use and storage in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) could flow to both SC PC and NGCC capture plants; the plant gate sales price hinges on, among other things, where the plant is and what crude oil costs. The cost of CO2 captured is the minimum plant gate sales price that would make carbon capture attractive instead of a defined non-capture reference plant. In Exhibit 5-9 it is read at the crossing of the PC capture lines with the SC PC non-capture line and of the NGCC capture line with the NGCC non-capture line: e.g., $58/tonne ($53/ton) for SC PC and $71/tonne ($64/ton) for NGCC. The curves use 85 percent capacity factor for PC and NGCC and fuel prices of $2.78/GJ ($2.94/MMBtu) for coal and $5.81/GJ ($6.13 /MMBtu) for gas. Exhibit 5-9 Impact of carbon sales price on study technologies (source: NETL).

From the carbon sales price graph: subcritical PC and SC PC respond indistinguishably to CO2 sales price, with and without capture; at baseline conditions a higher EOR sales price for CO2 benefits PC more than NGCC; and at $90/tonne the cost of NGCC with capture is almost equal to that of the subcritical and SC PC capture cases. As with emission pricing, a "phase diagram" type plot (Exhibit 5-10) of CO2 sales price against natural gas price shows COE parity lines between technology pairs. Exhibit 5-10 Lowest cost power generation options comparing NGCC and coal (source: NETL). Non-capture plants are cheapest below a first-year CO2 price of $56/tonne ($51/ton). NGCC is preferred with gas below $10/MMBtu and CO2 revenue below $56/tonne (85 percent capacity factor); the parity gas price between NGCC and PC cases falls at higher CO2 revenues, reaching $6/MMBtu at about $100/tonne ($91/ton).

Exhibit 5-11 plots COE sensitivity to fuel cost for the SC PC and NGCC cases. The SC PC bands cover a coal price range of $2.21 - $3.69/MMBtu (±25% around the study value of $2.94/MMBtu), revealing where NGCC competes with SCPC, with and without CCS, depending on delivered gas price. For example, at a coal cost of $3/MMBtu the non-capture SC PC COE equals the non-capture NGCC COE at a gas price of roughly $10/MMBtu, and the capture versions of SC PC and NGCC reach equal COE at $3/MMBtu coal and about $13.5/MMBtu gas. Exhibit 5-11 COE sensitivity to fuel costs (source: NETL; y-axis COE with CO2 T&S, $/MWh (2011$), x-axis delivered natural gas price, $/MMBtu).

Exhibit 5-12 shows COE versus CF for all technologies; the subcritical and SC PC curves practically coincide. CF ranges from 30 to 95 percent, the baseline being 85 percent for both PC and NGCC, and the curves assume CF could rise to 95 percent without extra capital equipment. High-capital technologies (PC with capture) see COE climb more steeply as CF falls, whereas non-capture NGCC stays fairly flat because its COE is dominated by fuel charges that shrink with CF. Conclusions: NGCC has the lowest non-capture COE at every CF shown; NGCC with capture has the lowest COE among capture technologies, and its lead widens as CF drops thanks to its relatively low capital component; near 60 percent CF, the COE of NGCC with capture crosses those of both non-capture PC cases, becoming higher than them as CF increases. Exhibit 5-12 COE sensitivity to capacity factor (source: NETL).
